items.title: What is NAV? Net Asset Value Meaning with Example
items.description: NAV meaning in mutual funds: how net asset value per unit is calculated, when it is declared, and why a low NAV does not make a fund cheap.
items.short: Net Asset Value (NAV) is the per-unit market value of a mutual fund scheme: total assets minus liabilities, divided by the number of units outstanding.
body: NAV is the price at which investors buy and sell units of an open-ended mutual fund scheme. The AMC values every security in the portfolio at the day's closing market price, adds cash and accrued income, subtracts liabilities such as expenses payable and redemption money owed, and divides the result by the number of units in issue.

Most schemes declare NAV once every business day, after markets close, and AMFI and the AMC websites publish it the same evening. Your purchase or redemption is processed at the NAV of the day your application and money reach the fund within the cut-off time, so you never know the exact price at the moment you place an order. This is called forward pricing and it protects existing investors from people trading on stale prices.

Each plan and option of a scheme has its own NAV. A direct plan carries a lower expense ratio than the regular plan of the same scheme, so its NAV grows slightly faster and the gap widens over the years.

The most common confusion is treating NAV like a share price. A fund with a NAV of ₹12 is not cheaper than one at ₹300. If both portfolios rise 10%, both NAVs rise 10% and your ₹10,000 grows to ₹11,000 either way. What matters is the change in NAV over time, the costs and the quality of the portfolio, not the NAV level itself. New fund offers launched at ₹10 are not bargains for the same reason.
items.example: An equity scheme holds shares worth ₹515 crore and cash of ₹5 crore, so total assets are ₹520 crore. It owes ₹20 crore (expenses payable and pending redemptions). Net assets are ₹500 crore. With 25 crore units outstanding, NAV = ₹500 crore ÷ 25 crore = ₹20 per unit. An investor putting in ₹50,000 that day receives 50,000 ÷ 20 = 2,500 units.
faqs: Is a mutual fund with a lower NAV better to buy?

No. NAV only reflects the value of the portfolio divided by units. A ₹15 NAV fund and a ₹500 NAV fund give the same percentage return if their portfolios move the same way. Compare funds on portfolio, consistency of returns, risk, costs and fit with your goal, not on the NAV level.
When is mutual fund NAV declared?

For most schemes NAV is computed and published every business day after market close, on the AMC website and AMFI's site. Some schemes such as fund of funds investing overseas may publish a little later because underlying prices arrive later. Check the scheme documents for exact timelines.

items.title: Asset Management Company (AMC) Meaning and Role
items.description: What an asset management company does in an Indian mutual fund, how it differs from the trustee and sponsor, and how it earns money from schemes.
items.short: An asset management company (AMC) is the SEBI-approved company that launches mutual fund schemes and manages their money as investment manager, under supervision of the fund's trustees.
body: In India a mutual fund is set up as a trust. The sponsor creates the trust, the trustees hold the assets for unit holders, and the trustees appoint an asset management company to run the schemes day to day. The AMC designs products, files scheme documents with SEBI, employs fund managers and research analysts, buys and sells securities, calculates NAV and handles investor service through registrars.

The AMC is paid out of the scheme's total expense ratio. That fee is charged as a percentage of assets under management, so an AMC earns more as AUM grows, whether from new money or market gains. It does not own the investors' money: securities sit with a separate custodian in the scheme's name, which is why a problem with an AMC's own finances does not directly put scheme assets at risk.

Every AMC must be approved by SEBI, maintain a minimum net worth, have independent directors on its board, and follow the SEBI (Mutual Funds) Regulations. Well-known Indian AMCs include those run by SBI, HDFC, ICICI Prudential and Nippon India.

Learners often mix up the AMC with the mutual fund itself. 'SBI Mutual Fund' is the trust; 'SBI Funds Management Ltd' is the AMC. Exam questions on the three-tier structure test exactly this distinction.
items.example: Suppose an AMC manages a flexi cap scheme with AUM of ₹8,000 crore and the scheme's expense ratio is 1.6% a year. Total expenses charged to the scheme are about ₹128 crore annually (₹8,000 crore × 1.6%), accrued daily into the NAV. Part of this covers distributor commission, registrar and custody costs; the remainder is the AMC's management fee. If AUM rises to ₹10,000 crore through market gains, the same percentage brings in more fee income.
faqs: Can an AMC run other businesses besides mutual funds?

SEBI allows AMCs to undertake certain other activities, such as portfolio management or advisory services to some categories of clients, only if there is no conflict of interest and they keep proper segregation. The exact list of permitted activities is set by SEBI regulations, so check the current rules before relying on a specific case.
What happens to my investment if an AMC shuts down?

Scheme assets are held by a custodian in the name of the scheme, not on the AMC's balance sheet. If an AMC exits, the trustees can transfer management of the schemes to another AMC or wind them up and return money at NAV, as per SEBI rules. Market losses in the portfolio, however, remain the investor's risk.

items.term: Three-tier structure of a mutual fund
items.title: Three-Tier Structure of Mutual Fund: Sponsor, Trustee, AMC
items.description: Understand the sponsor, trustee and AMC structure of Indian mutual funds, who appoints whom, and the role of the custodian and registrar.
items.short: The three-tier structure means an Indian mutual fund has a sponsor who sets it up, trustees who hold assets for investors, and an AMC that manages the money.
body: SEBI requires every mutual fund in India to be constituted as a trust under the Indian Trusts Act. This produces three layers. The sponsor is the promoter, much like a company's promoter, and must meet SEBI's eligibility norms on track record and net worth. The sponsor creates the trust and contributes to the AMC's capital.

The trustees, either a board of trustees or a trustee company, are the guardians of unit holders' interests. They appoint the AMC, approve schemes, monitor whether the AMC follows regulations and the scheme documents, and report to SEBI. A majority of trustees must be independent of the sponsor.

The AMC is the investment manager that actually runs the portfolios. Around these three sit service providers appointed with trustee approval: a custodian that holds securities, a registrar and transfer agent that maintains investor records, and auditors.

Why the separation? It prevents the people managing money from also controlling the safekeeping and supervision of that money. Exam questions often ask who appoints the AMC (the trustees, with SEBI approval), who holds securities (the custodian) and who is the settler of the trust (the sponsor). Remember that the investor's relationship is with the trust; units represent beneficial ownership in the scheme's assets.
items.example: Take a fictional group, Bharat Finserv Ltd. It acts as sponsor and sets up 'Bharat Mutual Fund' as a trust. It forms 'Bharat Trustee Company Pvt Ltd', where four of six directors are independent. The trustee company appoints 'Bharat Asset Management Ltd' as AMC. Securities bought by Bharat Bluechip Fund are held by a separate custodian bank, and investor folios are maintained by an RTA. If the AMC breaches an investment limit, the trustees must act and report it.
faqs: Who appoints the AMC of a mutual fund?

The trustees appoint the AMC through an investment management agreement, and SEBI must approve the AMC. The sponsor sets up the trust and usually promotes the AMC, but the formal appointment and ongoing supervision are trustee responsibilities. This is a frequently tested point in NISM mutual fund exams.
Is the custodian part of the three tiers?

No. The three tiers are sponsor, trustee and AMC. The custodian is a service provider that holds the scheme's securities and settles trades. It is appointed with trustee approval and should be independent of the sponsor to avoid conflicts, subject to conditions laid down by SEBI.

items.title: What is SIP? Systematic Investment Plan Meaning
items.description: SIP meaning explained: how a systematic investment plan buys mutual fund units every month, how auto-debit works, and what SIP can and cannot do.
items.short: A Systematic Investment Plan (SIP) is a facility to invest a fixed amount in a mutual fund scheme at regular intervals, usually monthly, through an automatic bank debit.
body: A SIP is not a product; it is a way of investing in an ordinary mutual fund scheme. You choose the scheme, amount, date and frequency, register a bank mandate (NACH or UPI AutoPay), and on each date the amount is debited and units are allotted at that day's applicable NAV.

Because the amount is fixed and the NAV varies, you buy more units when prices are low and fewer when they are high. Over time this gives an average purchase cost below the simple average of NAVs, a result called rupee cost averaging. More importantly, a SIP turns investing into a habit that does not depend on reading the market.

SIPs can be paused, modified or stopped, generally with notice of a few days to the AMC. Missing an instalment because of low bank balance usually carries no penalty from the fund, though your bank may charge a bounce fee and repeated failures can lead to cancellation. A step-up or top-up SIP raises the instalment every year, often in line with salary growth.

Common misconceptions: a SIP does not guarantee positive returns, does not by itself reduce risk in a falling market that never recovers, and is not tied to a lock-in unless the scheme is ELSS, where each instalment is locked for three years from its own date. Each instalment is also a separate purchase for capital gains tax.
items.example: Riya starts a ₹5,000 monthly SIP in an equity index fund. In month 1 NAV is ₹100 and she gets 50 units. In month 2 NAV falls to ₹80 and she gets 62.5 units. In month 3 NAV is ₹125, giving 40 units. After three months she has invested ₹15,000 and holds 152.5 units, an average cost of about ₹98.36 per unit, below the simple average NAV of ₹101.67.
faqs: What is the minimum amount for a SIP?

It depends on the scheme. Many funds accept monthly SIPs from ₹500, and several allow ₹100 or similar small amounts. The minimum is stated in the scheme information document and on the AMC website, and SEBI has also encouraged small-ticket SIPs, so check the current scheme terms.
Is SIP better than a lump sum?

Neither is always better. A lump sum invested before a sustained rise does better; a SIP smooths entry when markets are volatile and suits people investing from monthly income. For money already in hand, many investors use an STP to spread entry. The right choice depends on cash flows and risk comfort.

items.title: Rupee Cost Averaging: Meaning, Formula and Example
items.description: How rupee cost averaging works in SIPs, why your average cost ends up below the average NAV, and its limits when markets fall or rise steadily.
items.short: Rupee cost averaging is the effect of investing a fixed rupee amount at regular intervals, so more units are bought at low prices and fewer at high prices.
body: When you invest the same amount every period, the number of units you get is amount ÷ price. Low prices give more units and high prices give fewer. Your average cost per unit is the total invested divided by total units, which mathematically equals the harmonic mean of the prices paid. The harmonic mean is always at or below the simple average, so your average cost is lower than the average NAV over the period.

This does not mean you always make money. If a fund keeps falling, you keep buying at lower prices and your total value can still be below your investment. If a fund rises steadily, a lump sum at the start would have bought more units cheaply, and averaging gives a worse result.

The real benefit is behavioural. Investors who average do not need to time the market, and a fall stops being frightening because it buys more units. That is why the concept is taught in NISM mutual fund and adviser exams alongside SIPs.

Do not confuse rupee cost averaging with 'averaging down' in stocks, where someone buys more of a losing share hoping to reduce cost. Rupee cost averaging is a fixed, pre-decided schedule, not a reaction to losses.
items.example: An investor puts ₹5,000 each month for five months into a fund whose NAV moves ₹50, ₹40, ₹25, ₹40, ₹50. Units bought: 100, 125, 200, 125 and 100, a total of 650 units for ₹25,000. Average cost = ₹25,000 ÷ 650 = ₹38.46. The simple average NAV is (50+40+25+40+50) ÷ 5 = ₹41. At the end NAV is back to ₹50, so the holding is worth ₹32,500, a gain of ₹7,500 even though NAV only returned to where it started.
faqs: Does rupee cost averaging reduce risk?

It reduces timing risk, the risk of putting all your money in at a market peak. It does not remove market risk: if the underlying assets fall and stay down, a SIP investor still loses money. Think of it as smoothing the entry price, not protecting the investment.
Why is the average cost lower than the average NAV?

Because you buy more units when NAV is low. Those cheaper units carry more weight in your average. Mathematically your cost is the harmonic mean of prices, which is never higher than the arithmetic mean. The gap is wider when prices swing more.

items.title: What is SWP? Systematic Withdrawal Plan Explained
items.description: SWP meaning: how a systematic withdrawal plan pays you a fixed amount from a mutual fund, how it is taxed, and how long a corpus can last.
items.short: A Systematic Withdrawal Plan (SWP) lets an investor redeem a fixed amount or the appreciation from a mutual fund scheme at regular intervals, creating a steady cash flow.
body: An SWP is the mirror image of a SIP. You hold units in a scheme and instruct the AMC to redeem enough units each month or quarter to pay a fixed sum into your bank account. Retirees use it to draw a 'salary' from a corpus, and parents use it to pay college fees over several years.

Each withdrawal is a redemption. The AMC sells units at that day's NAV, so the number of units sold varies: more units go when NAV is low. Only the gain portion of each redemption is taxable as capital gain, which is why an SWP is often more tax-efficient than an IDCW payout where the full distribution is taxed at slab rate.

The key risk is sequence of returns. If markets fall sharply in the early years while you keep withdrawing, you sell many units cheaply and the corpus may not recover. Retirement advisers therefore keep two or three years of withdrawals in debt or liquid funds and run the SWP from there.

An SWP is not a guaranteed pension. If the withdrawal rate is higher than the portfolio's return, the corpus shrinks and eventually runs out. Exit loads may apply to units redeemed within the load period.
items.example: Mr. Iyer, 62, has ₹20 lakh in a conservative hybrid fund and sets up an SWP of ₹15,000 a month (₹1.8 lakh a year, 9% of the corpus). If the fund earns 8% a year, compounded monthly, the corpus would still be about ₹16.95 lakh after 10 years and would last roughly 331 months, about 27.5 years. If returns were lower or he withdrew more, it would run out much sooner. These figures are illustrations, not projections.
faqs: Is SWP income taxable?

Only the capital gain inside each withdrawal is taxed, not the full amount. Part of every redemption is your own original investment returning to you. Whether the gain is short or long term depends on how long those specific units were held, using first-in-first-out. Tax rules change, so check current income tax department guidance.
How much can I withdraw through an SWP safely?

There is no single safe figure. It depends on the corpus, expected return, inflation and how many years the money must last. Many planners test withdrawal rates of around 3–5% a year for long retirements. A registered investment adviser can model your situation; the fund house itself will not set the rate for you.

items.title: What is STP in Mutual Funds? Systematic Transfer Plan
items.description: STP meaning in mutual funds: how a systematic transfer plan moves money from a liquid or debt fund to an equity fund in instalments, with an example.
items.short: A Systematic Transfer Plan (STP) automatically moves a fixed amount at regular intervals from one scheme to another scheme of the same mutual fund house.
body: An STP is used when an investor has a lump sum but does not want to put it into equity at one go. The money is first parked in a low-volatility scheme, usually a liquid, overnight or ultra short duration fund. On each STP date, units of the source scheme are redeemed and the proceeds are invested in the target scheme, so the investor gets SIP-like averaging without needing monthly bank debits.

Both schemes must belong to the same AMC. Each transfer is legally a redemption from the source and a purchase in the target, so capital gains on the source units become taxable and any exit load on the source applies. Liquid funds have only a tiny graded exit load for the first week, which is why they are popular sources.

A reverse use is also common: as a goal approaches, investors run an STP from an equity fund into a debt fund to lock in gains gradually. Variants include fixed STP, capital appreciation STP (only the gains are moved) and flexi STP, where the amount depends on market conditions as per the AMC's formula.
STP is not a guarantee against loss. If the equity market rises steadily during the transfer period, an immediate lump sum would have done better.
items.example: Neha receives a ₹6 lakh bonus. She invests it in a liquid fund and sets up an STP of ₹50,000 a month into a large cap fund for 12 months. Each month about ₹50,000 of liquid fund units are redeemed and large cap units are bought at that day's NAV. The money waiting in the liquid fund keeps earning short-term debt returns, and her equity entry is spread across a year of market ups and downs.
faqs: Can I do an STP between two different AMCs?

No. An STP works only between schemes of the same mutual fund house because the AMC processes the redemption and purchase internally. To move money between fund houses you must redeem from one and invest in the other yourself, or set up a SWP into your bank and a separate SIP.
Is STP taxable?

Yes. Every transfer is a redemption from the source scheme, so any gain on the source units is a capital gain for that financial year. Gains on liquid funds over a few months are usually small, but they are still taxable at the applicable rate. Keep records of each transfer for filing returns.

items.title: Expense Ratio (TER) in Mutual Funds: Meaning and Impact
items.description: What the total expense ratio of a mutual fund includes, how it is charged daily through NAV, and how a 1% difference compounds over 20 years.
items.short: Total expense ratio (TER) is the annual cost of running a mutual fund scheme, shown as a percentage of its average assets and deducted daily from the NAV.
body: TER covers the AMC's management fee, distributor commission (in regular plans), registrar and custodian fees, audit, marketing and other operating costs, along with GST on management fees. You never receive a bill. Instead, one-365th of the annual rate is accrued every day, so the NAV you see is already net of expenses.

SEBI caps TER in slabs that fall as a scheme's AUM rises, with different ceilings for equity, debt, index funds and fund of funds. SEBI has revised the TER framework more than once, so check the current Mutual Fund Regulations and AMFI disclosures for exact limits as of 2026. AMCs must publish each scheme's TER on their website and give advance notice to investors before increasing it.

Brokerage paid on trades within the portfolio is partly outside the headline figure, and exit loads are separate. A direct plan has a lower TER than the regular plan of the same scheme because it pays no distributor commission.

The misconception is that small percentages do not matter. Costs are certain while returns are not, and the difference compounds on a growing base every year. For passive funds, where portfolios are almost identical across AMCs, TER is one of the main differences between choices.
items.example: Two investors each put ₹10 lakh into funds whose portfolios earn 12% a year before costs. Fund A charges 1.5% TER, so the net return is about 10.5%; Fund B charges 0.5%, so the net return is about 11.5%. After 20 years Fund A grows to roughly ₹73.7 lakh and Fund B to roughly ₹88.2 lakh. The 1 percentage point difference in cost costs about ₹14.5 lakh, more than the original investment.
faqs: Is expense ratio deducted from my investment amount?

No. You are not charged separately. The expense is accrued daily within the scheme and reduces the NAV slightly every day. That is why returns reported by funds are already after expenses. Your statement shows units and NAV, not a separate fee line.
Is a low expense ratio fund always better?

Not automatically. For index funds and ETFs tracking the same index, lower TER and lower tracking error usually make one fund better. For actively managed funds, quality of management also matters. But a higher fee must be earned back through better performance every year, which is a high bar.

items.title: Exit Load in Mutual Funds: Meaning and Calculation
items.description: What exit load means in mutual funds, how it is calculated on redemption value, typical structures, and how SIP instalments are treated separately.
items.short: Exit load is a fee, expressed as a percentage of redemption value, that a mutual fund deducts when units are redeemed or switched out before a specified holding period.
body: AMCs use exit loads to discourage short-term trading that can disturb the portfolio and hurt long-term investors. A common equity fund structure is 1% if units are redeemed within 12 months of allotment and nil afterwards. Debt funds often have shorter periods or none, and liquid funds carry a graded load only for the first six days.

The load is applied to the redemption value, not the gain. The fund pays you NAV minus the load, and under SEBI rules the exit load collected is credited back to the scheme, which benefits remaining investors. GST on the load is handled as per tax rules.

Each purchase, including each SIP instalment, has its own allotment date. If you redeem, units are treated on a first-in-first-out basis, so the oldest units go first. Some may be beyond the load period and others within it.

There is no entry load in India; SEBI abolished it in 2009. Switches between schemes and between plans of the same scheme are redemptions and can attract exit load. Exit load structures can be changed by the AMC, but the load applicable at the time you invested generally applies to those units. Check the scheme information document and KIM before investing.
items.example: Arjun invested ₹2 lakh in an equity fund at NAV ₹40, getting 5,000 units. The exit load is 1% within one year. After nine months the NAV is ₹44, so redemption value is 5,000 × ₹44 = ₹2,20,000. Exit load = 1% × ₹2,20,000 = ₹2,200. He receives ₹2,17,800 (before any tax). Had he waited three more months, there would have been no load.
faqs: Is exit load charged on SIPs?

Yes, but separately for each instalment. Each SIP instalment has its own allotment date and the load period runs from that date. If you redeem everything after 13 months on a one-year load, the first instalment is load-free while the last 12 instalments still attract the load.
Who keeps the exit load money?

Under current SEBI rules, the exit load collected is credited to the scheme itself, net of applicable GST, rather than kept by the AMC. This compensates the remaining investors for transaction costs caused by early exits. Check current SEBI circulars for any updates.

items.title: Direct vs Regular Mutual Fund Plan: Key Differences
items.description: Direct plan vs regular plan explained: same portfolio, different expense ratio, NAV and distributor role. Learn which suits whom with an example.
items.short: A direct plan is a mutual fund plan bought straight from the AMC without a distributor, while a regular plan is bought through a distributor and has a higher expense ratio.
body: Since January 2013 SEBI has required every mutual fund scheme to offer a direct plan alongside the regular plan. Both plans invest in exactly the same portfolio and are managed by the same fund manager. The only difference is cost: the regular plan's expense ratio includes the commission paid to the distributor, while the direct plan does not.
Because the direct plan has lower expenses, its NAV grows a little faster each day. Over long periods the gap compounds, so the two plans of the same scheme show different NAVs and different returns.

Direct plans can be bought on the AMC website, through registrar platforms, through stock exchange platforms or via SEBI-registered investment advisers who charge a separate fee. Regular plans come with a distributor who may help with paperwork, scheme selection and hand-holding during market falls, and that service is paid for through the commission.

The common misunderstanding is that a direct plan is a different or 'safer' fund. It is not. Another trap: moving from regular to direct is a redemption plus purchase, so it can trigger exit load and capital gains tax. Investors should weigh the cost saving against these one-time costs and against the value of advice they receive.
items.example: A flexi cap scheme's regular plan has a TER of 1.7% and its direct plan 0.7%. Suppose the portfolio earns 13% before costs. ₹5 lakh in the regular plan grows at about 11.3% net, reaching about ₹14.6 lakh in 10 years. In the direct plan it grows at about 12.3%, reaching about ₹15.9 lakh. The roughly ₹1.3 lakh difference is the cost of distribution over the decade.
faqs: Is a direct plan riskier than a regular plan?

No. The risk is identical because both plans hold the same portfolio. The difference is only the expense ratio and whether a distributor is attached to your folio. Any risk comes from the scheme's investments, which are the same in both plans.
Can a mutual fund distributor sell direct plans?

A distributor earns commission only on regular plans. Under SEBI's framework, advice on direct plans for a fee is meant for SEBI-registered investment advisers, while distributors may offer execution-only services on direct plans in limited ways. Rules on this have evolved, so check current SEBI circulars.

items.term: IDCW option (Income Distribution cum Capital Withdrawal)
items.title: IDCW Meaning in Mutual Funds: IDCW vs Growth Option
items.description: IDCW full form and meaning: why the old dividend option was renamed, how payouts reduce NAV, how they are taxed, and how IDCW compares with growth.
items.short: IDCW, or Income Distribution cum Capital Withdrawal, is the mutual fund option (earlier called the dividend option) under which the scheme pays out part of its distributable surplus to unit holders.
body: Every mutual fund plan offers a growth option and usually an IDCW option. Under growth, all gains stay in the scheme and show up as a rising NAV. Under IDCW, the trustees may declare a distribution from time to time; the NAV falls by the amount paid out, and investors receive cash (payout) or extra units (reinvestment).

SEBI renamed the 'dividend' option to IDCW from April 2021 because the old name misled investors. A mutual fund 'dividend' is not extra profit like a company dividend; it is often your own capital being handed back. Part of each distribution can come from the equalisation reserve built out of money that new investors paid in.

Taxation tilts the choice for most people. Since April 2020, IDCW is taxable in the investor's hands at slab rate, and the fund deducts TDS above a threshold. Under the growth option, tax arises only on redemption and only on the gain, at capital gains rates. For an investor in a higher slab, growth plus a planned SWP is often more efficient than IDCW payouts.
IDCW is neither fixed nor assured. The amount and frequency depend on available surplus and the trustees' decision, and payouts can stop entirely.
items.example: Kavita holds 10,000 units of a hybrid fund's IDCW option at NAV ₹25 (value ₹2,50,000). The fund declares IDCW of ₹1 per unit. She receives ₹10,000, and the NAV falls to about ₹24, so her holding is now worth ₹2,40,000. Her total wealth is unchanged at ₹2,50,000, but the ₹10,000 is added to her income and taxed at her slab rate. Had she chosen growth, nothing would be taxed until she redeemed.
faqs: Is IDCW better than growth for regular income?

Not necessarily. IDCW payouts are irregular and taxed fully at slab rate. A growth option with a systematic withdrawal plan gives a predictable amount and taxes only the gain portion of each withdrawal. Investors in low tax brackets may find the difference small; those in higher slabs usually find SWP more efficient.
Does NAV fall after IDCW is declared?

Yes. On the record date the NAV of the IDCW option falls by the amount distributed plus any statutory levy. This is why an IDCW does not add to your wealth; it only moves money from the fund to your bank account.

items.title: Growth Option in Mutual Funds: Meaning and Benefits
items.description: What the growth option in a mutual fund means, how returns compound inside NAV, how it is taxed only on redemption, and when it suits investors.
items.short: The growth option is a mutual fund choice under which no income is paid out; all earnings remain invested and are reflected in a rising NAV.
body: When you pick the growth option, interest, dividends received from companies and realised gains stay inside the scheme. Your number of units stays the same and the NAV rises over time, so the value of your holding is simply units × current NAV. The compounding happens quietly inside the fund.

Tax is deferred until you redeem. Only then is the gain (sale value minus purchase cost) taxed as short or long term capital gain, depending on the scheme type and holding period. Nothing is taxed while you hold. This makes growth the default choice for long-term goals such as retirement or a child's education.

The growth option of a scheme and its IDCW option share the same portfolio and expense ratio within a plan, but have different NAVs because the IDCW NAV drops each time a payout is made. Comparing returns across these options without adjusting for payouts gives misleading results.

Investors who need cash flow can still choose growth and set up a systematic withdrawal plan. One mistake is assuming growth means a 'growth stock' strategy; it says nothing about how the fund invests, only what happens to its earnings.
items.example: Sameer invests ₹1,00,000 in the growth option of an equity fund at NAV ₹50, getting 2,000 units. Five years later the NAV is ₹88. His holding is worth 2,000 × ₹88 = ₹1,76,000. He paid no tax during these years. If he redeems now, his long-term gain is ₹76,000, taxed under the equity LTCG rules for that year after any available exemption.
faqs: Can I switch from IDCW to growth in the same scheme?

Yes, but it is treated as a redemption from the IDCW option and a fresh purchase in the growth option. That may trigger exit load if within the load period, and capital gains tax on the units redeemed. Check costs before switching.
Why do growth and IDCW options have different NAVs?

Both start at the same NAV, but every IDCW payout reduces the IDCW option's NAV. The growth option keeps all earnings, so its NAV ends up higher. The underlying portfolio and returns before payouts are the same.

items.title: Open-Ended Mutual Fund: Meaning, Features, Example
items.description: What an open-ended mutual fund is, how units are created and cancelled daily at NAV, why liquidity is high, and how it differs from a close-ended fund.
items.short: An open-ended fund is a mutual fund scheme that issues and redeems units on every business day at NAV, with no fixed maturity or limit on unit capital.
body: Most mutual fund schemes in India are open-ended. After the new fund offer closes, the scheme reopens within a short period for continuous sale and repurchase. When an investor buys, new units are created; when an investor redeems, units are cancelled. The size of the fund therefore expands and shrinks with investor flows.

Liquidity comes directly from the AMC. You do not need a buyer on an exchange; the fund itself pays you at the applicable NAV, usually within a few working days for equity schemes (SEBI sets maximum timelines) and faster for liquid funds. There is no maturity date, so you can hold for decades.

The flip side is that the fund manager must keep some cash and liquid securities to meet redemptions. Heavy outflows during a market fall can force selling at poor prices, which hurts remaining investors. Exit loads and, in extreme cases, SEBI-permitted restrictions on redemption help manage this.
Open-ended does not mean free of lock-in: ELSS is open-ended yet each unit is locked for three years. Nor does it mean units trade on an exchange; that is the feature of ETFs and close-ended funds.
items.example: A large cap fund has 10 crore units and NAV ₹30, so AUM is ₹300 crore. On Monday investors buy ₹6 crore and redeem ₹3 crore at that day's NAV of ₹30. The fund issues 20 lakh new units and cancels 10 lakh units, ending with 10.1 crore units and AUM of ₹303 crore. Nothing had to trade on a stock exchange.
faqs: Can an open-ended fund stop redemptions?

Only in exceptional situations and as permitted by SEBI, for example severe market disruption or liquidity crisis, and subject to conditions such as trustee approval and time limits. In normal conditions an open-ended fund must honour redemptions at NAV within the prescribed time.
Is an open-ended fund better than a close-ended fund?

Open-ended funds offer daily liquidity and the option to invest through SIPs, which suits most retail investors. Close-ended funds lock money for a fixed term, which can help managers invest in less liquid securities. Which suits you depends on your need for liquidity and the strategy.

items.title: Close-Ended Fund Meaning: Features and Exit Options
items.description: Close-ended mutual fund meaning: fixed maturity, units sold only in the NFO, mandatory stock exchange listing, and why units can trade at a discount.
items.short: A close-ended fund is a mutual fund scheme with a fixed maturity whose units are sold only during the new fund offer and are not redeemed by the AMC before maturity.
body: A close-ended scheme raises money once, through its NFO, and then invests for a stated tenure such as three or five years. The unit capital is fixed after the offer. Investors cannot buy more units from the AMC later and cannot ask the AMC to buy units back before maturity.

To give investors an exit, SEBI requires close-ended schemes to list their units on a recognised stock exchange. In practice trading volumes are often thin, and units may change hands at a discount to NAV. On maturity, the scheme is wound up or converted and investors receive the NAV of that date.

Fixed maturity plans (FMPs) are the best-known close-ended debt schemes; they buy bonds maturing close to the scheme's own maturity, which reduces interest rate risk if held to the end. Some close-ended equity funds use the fixed tenure to invest in smaller, less liquid companies without worrying about redemptions.

A frequent confusion: a close-ended fund is not a guaranteed-return product. FMP brochures show 'indicative' yields, but returns depend on the actual portfolio and defaults can occur. NAV is still disclosed regularly even though you cannot redeem at it daily.
items.example: An FMP with a 1,100-day tenure raises ₹400 crore at ₹10 per unit and buys bonds maturing just before the scheme. After a year its NAV is ₹10.80, but on the exchange units trade at ₹10.50 because few buyers exist. An investor who must exit now loses about 2.8% versus NAV. Another who holds to maturity receives the final NAV, say ₹12.30, directly from the fund.
faqs: Can I sell close-ended fund units before maturity?

Yes, by selling them on the stock exchange where they are listed, through your demat account and broker. The AMC itself will not redeem them early. Liquidity can be thin, so you may have to accept a price below NAV.
Why do close-ended funds trade at a discount?

Low trading volumes, few buyers and the lock-in until maturity make investors demand a lower price. The discount usually narrows as maturity approaches because the payout at NAV becomes near and certain.

items.title: Interval Fund Meaning: How Transaction Windows Work
items.description: What an interval fund is, how its specified transaction periods work, its listing requirement, and how it sits between open- and close-ended funds.
items.short: An interval fund is a mutual fund scheme that combines close-ended and open-ended features, allowing purchases and redemptions only during pre-specified transaction intervals.
body: Between transaction windows an interval fund behaves like a close-ended scheme: no fresh subscriptions and no redemptions with the AMC. During the specified transaction period, which SEBI requires to be at least a few business days, investors can buy or redeem units at NAV. The windows recur at intervals stated in the scheme information document, such as every quarter or year.
Like close-ended schemes, interval fund units must be listed on a stock exchange so investors have some exit route outside the windows, although trading is usually limited.

The structure helps a fund manager match the portfolio to known liquidity dates. A debt interval fund with quarterly windows can buy instruments maturing around those dates, reducing the need for distress selling. SEBI also limits how far the portfolio's maturity can extend beyond the next interval.
Interval funds are relatively rare in India today, but they are a standard exam topic. Do not confuse them with schemes that simply have lock-ins (ELSS) or with SIP intervals.
items.example: A debt interval fund has a transaction window from 1 to 5 March, June, September and December. Ravi invests ₹2 lakh on 3 June at NAV ₹20, getting 10,000 units. In August he needs cash; the AMC will not redeem, so he can sell on the exchange or wait. On 2 September he redeems directly at that day's NAV of ₹20.35, receiving ₹2,03,500.
faqs: Is an interval fund open-ended or close-ended?

SEBI's classification treats it as a hybrid of the two. It is close-ended between transaction periods and allows entry and exit like an open-ended fund during specified windows. Exam questions often describe it as a fund with features of both.
Why must interval funds be listed?

Listing gives investors a way to exit between transaction windows by selling to another investor on the exchange. Without it, investors could be stuck until the next interval. Actual liquidity on the exchange may be limited.

items.title: ELSS Meaning: Tax Saving Mutual Fund and 3-Year Lock-in
items.description: ELSS explained: how this tax-saving equity mutual fund works, its 3-year lock-in, deduction under the old tax regime, and how SIP lock-in is counted.
items.short: An Equity Linked Savings Scheme (ELSS) is a diversified equity mutual fund with a three-year lock-in that qualifies for the Section 80C deduction under the old tax regime.
body: ELSS is the only mutual fund category eligible for the familiar 80C deduction, alongside PPF, EPF, life insurance premiums and others within the overall annual limit (₹1.5 lakh as of 2026). SEBI requires an ELSS to invest at least 80% in equities. Each AMC may run only one ELSS scheme.

Every investment is locked in for three years from the date of allotment. With a SIP, each instalment has its own three-year clock, so the last instalment unlocks three years after it was made. After lock-in the units can be held as long as you wish.

The deduction is available only under the old tax regime. Under the new default regime there is no 80C deduction, so ELSS becomes simply an equity fund with a lock-in. On redemption, gains are taxed as equity long-term capital gains because the holding always exceeds one year. Note also that the Income-tax Act, 2025 replaces the 1961 Act from April 2026 and renumbers sections, so check the current reference for this deduction.

Compared with other 80C options, ELSS has the shortest lock-in but the highest volatility. It is unsuitable for anyone whose money is needed in exactly three years, since equity can be down at that moment.
items.example: Pooja, under the old regime in the 30% slab, invests ₹1,50,000 in ELSS through a monthly SIP of ₹12,500. Her taxable income falls by ₹1.5 lakh, saving about ₹46,800 in tax including 4% cess (₹1,50,000 × 31.2%), assuming no other 80C investments. Her April instalment unlocks next on that date three years later, her March instalment a year after that.
faqs: Can I withdraw ELSS before three years?

No. The three-year lock-in is mandatory and applies to each purchase separately. Only in the case of the investor's death can the nominee or legal heir redeem earlier, after one year from allotment, as per the scheme terms. Plan ELSS investments with money you will not need for at least three years.
Is ELSS useful under the new tax regime?

The new regime does not allow the 80C deduction, so there is no tax saving on investment. ELSS still works as a diversified equity fund, but the lock-in becomes a restriction without a matching benefit. Compare it with other flexi cap or index funds before choosing.

items.title: What is an Index Fund? Meaning, Costs and Example
items.description: Index fund meaning: how a passive mutual fund copies an index like Nifty 50, why costs and tracking error matter, and how it differs from an ETF.
items.short: An index fund is a passively managed mutual fund that holds the same securities as a chosen market index, in the same proportions, aiming to match the index's return.
body: Instead of a fund manager picking stocks, an index fund simply replicates an index such as the Nifty 50, Sensex or Nifty Next 50. When the index provider changes constituents or weights, the fund adjusts. SEBI requires index funds to invest at least 95% of assets in the securities of the underlying index.

Because no research team is needed to pick securities, expense ratios are low. The fund will slightly underperform its index because of expenses, cash held for redemptions and timing of trades. This shortfall is measured by tracking difference, and its variability by tracking error; AMCs disclose both.

Index funds are bought and sold with the AMC at NAV, just like any open-ended fund, so SIPs are easy and no demat account is required. That is the main practical difference from an ETF, which trades on the exchange throughout the day.

Investors often assume an index fund is low-risk. It carries full market risk of its index: a Nifty 50 index fund falls as much as the Nifty in a crash. Its promise is market return at low cost, not protection. Different index funds on the same index can still differ in returns because of cost and tracking efficiency.
items.example: Two Nifty 50 index funds track the same index. Over one year the Nifty 50 Total Return Index rises 14.0%. Fund X, with 0.20% TER and tight tracking, returns 13.75%. Fund Y, with 0.50% TER and more cash drag, returns 13.35%. On ₹5 lakh, the gap is about ₹2,000 in a single year, purely from implementation.
faqs: Is an index fund better than an actively managed fund?

It depends on the category. In large caps, many active funds have found it hard to beat the index after costs, so index funds are popular there. In less efficient segments some active funds have done better. An index fund offers predictable relative performance; an active fund offers a chance of outperformance with the risk of underperformance.
Do I need a demat account for an index fund?
No. An index fund is a regular mutual fund scheme bought from the AMC or through a distributor or platform at NAV. A demat account is needed only for ETFs, which trade on stock exchanges.

items.title: What is an ETF? Exchange Traded Fund Meaning in India
items.description: ETF meaning: how exchange traded funds trade on NSE and BSE like shares, how iNAV and market makers work, and how ETFs differ from index funds.
items.short: An exchange traded fund (ETF) is a mutual fund scheme, usually passive, whose units are listed and traded on a stock exchange at market prices throughout the trading day.
body: An ETF holds a basket of securities that tracks an index, gold, silver or a bond index. Retail investors buy and sell ETF units on NSE or BSE through a broker and a demat account, at the live market price, just like shares. Large participants called authorised participants and market makers can create or redeem units directly with the AMC in big blocks.

Because units trade on the market, the price can differ slightly from the underlying value. Exchanges and AMCs publish an indicative NAV (iNAV) during market hours so investors can judge whether the market price is fair. In liquid ETFs the gap is tiny; in thinly traded ETFs it can be meaningful.

ETFs generally have very low expense ratios, but investors pay brokerage, demat charges and the bid-ask spread. SIPs are possible only through brokers that offer them, since the AMC does not run regular-sized ETF SIPs directly.

Popular Indian ETFs include Nifty 50, Bank Nifty, gold and Bharat Bond ETFs. A common confusion is to think every ETF is equity; gold and debt ETFs exist too. Another is to ignore liquidity: always check traded volume and spread before buying.
items.example: A Nifty 50 ETF has a NAV of ₹245.10 and an iNAV of ₹245.30 at 11 a.m. On the exchange the best bid is ₹245.20 and best offer ₹245.40. Anil buys 400 units at ₹245.40, paying ₹98,160 plus brokerage. If the ETF were illiquid with an offer at ₹249, he would be overpaying by about 1.5% versus iNAV, which is why he checks the spread first.
faqs: What is the difference between an ETF and an index fund?

Both can track the same index. An index fund is bought from the AMC at end-of-day NAV, needs no demat account and suits SIPs. An ETF trades on the exchange at live prices, needs a demat and broking account, and involves brokerage and bid-ask spreads but often has a lower expense ratio.
What is iNAV in an ETF?

iNAV, or indicative NAV, is an estimate of the ETF's per-unit value computed through the trading day from live prices of its holdings. It helps investors check whether the market price is close to fair value. AMCs and exchanges publish it at regular intervals.

items.title: Fund of Funds (FoF) Meaning: Domestic and Overseas FoF
items.description: What a fund of funds is, how it invests in other mutual fund schemes or overseas funds, the double layer of costs, and how it is taxed in India.
items.short: A fund of funds (FoF) is a mutual fund scheme that invests mainly in units of other mutual fund schemes or ETFs rather than directly in shares or bonds.
body: An FoF builds its portfolio out of other funds. A domestic FoF might hold a mix of equity, debt and gold ETFs to create a multi-asset portfolio. An overseas FoF invests in a foreign mutual fund or ETF, giving Indian investors access to US or global markets in rupees through an ordinary folio. Gold and silver FoFs invest in the corresponding ETFs so that investors without a demat account can participate.

Costs come in two layers: the FoF's own expense ratio and the expenses of the underlying schemes. SEBI caps the combined TER for FoFs, but total cost can still be higher than buying the underlying fund directly. Investors should look at the total, which AMCs disclose.

Overseas FoFs are subject to industry-wide limits on foreign investment set by SEBI and RBI. When the limits were reached in 2022, several AMCs stopped accepting fresh money, which surprised investors who had running SIPs.

Tax treatment of an FoF depends on how much it invests in domestic equity; most FoFs do not qualify as equity-oriented and are taxed under non-equity rules that have changed several times recently. Check current income tax rules as of 2026 before assuming a rate.
items.example: An asset allocation FoF invests ₹100 crore as 50% in a Nifty 50 ETF, 30% in a short duration fund and 20% in a gold ETF. Its own TER is 0.15% and the weighted TER of its holdings is about 0.35%, so the total annual cost is roughly 0.50%. An investor putting ₹2 lakh into this FoF gets a three-asset portfolio, rebalanced by the fund manager, through one scheme and one NAV.
faqs: Why do fund of funds have higher costs?

Investors bear the FoF's own expenses plus the expenses charged inside each underlying scheme. Even though SEBI caps the total, the combination is often higher than investing in a single fund directly. The convenience of one-stop allocation or overseas access is what the extra cost buys.
Do I need a demat account for a gold FoF?

No. A gold FoF is a regular mutual fund scheme that invests in gold ETFs. You buy it from the AMC at NAV, like any other fund, and can use SIPs. To buy a gold ETF directly you would need a demat and broking account.

items.title: Liquid Fund Meaning: Uses, Maturity Limit and Exit Load
items.description: Liquid fund explained: debt fund investing up to 91 days maturity, graded exit load for 7 days, cut-off timing and why it suits emergency money.
items.short: A liquid fund is an open-ended debt mutual fund that invests only in money market and debt securities with maturity of up to 91 days.
body: Liquid funds hold treasury bills, commercial paper, certificates of deposit, repos and short-term government securities. Because maturities are so short, interest rate movements hardly affect the NAV, and the NAV generally rises a little almost every day. SEBI also requires liquid funds to keep a part of assets in cash-like instruments and to value holdings on a mark-to-market basis.

NAV is declared for every calendar day, including weekends and holidays. Applications for liquid funds have an earlier cut-off (1:30 pm) than other schemes, and you get the previous day's NAV only if money is credited to the fund before the cut-off. Redemptions are usually paid the next business day, and many AMCs offer instant redemption up to a small limit.
SEBI mandates a graded exit load for the first six days to discourage very short-term arbitrage by large investors. From day seven there is no load.

Liquid funds are low-risk, not risk-free. In 2019–2020, defaults in some commercial paper caused sharp one-day NAV drops in a few schemes. Check the credit quality of the portfolio and the scheme's risk-o-meter. Gains are taxed at slab rate as of 2026 under the rules for debt schemes bought after April 2023.
items.example: Meera parks ₹3 lakh of her emergency fund in a liquid fund instead of a savings account. On a day her NAV is ₹4,000, she gets 75 units. She needs ₹40,000 on day 4. The graded exit load for day 4 is 0.0055%, so she pays about ₹2.20. If she redeemed on day 7 or later, she would pay nothing.
faqs: Is a liquid fund safer than a savings account?

They carry different risks. A bank savings deposit is covered by DICGC deposit insurance up to a limit and has no NAV fluctuation. A liquid fund has no such insurance and carries small credit and liquidity risk, though it may earn more. Many people split emergency money between the two.
What is the exit load on liquid funds?

SEBI prescribes a graded load for redemptions within six days: 0.0070% on day 1 falling by 0.0005% each day to 0.0045% on day 6, and nil from day 7. The amounts are tiny for small investors. Check the scheme documents for any changes.

items.title: Overnight Fund Meaning: Lowest-Risk Debt Fund Category
items.description: What an overnight fund invests in, why its securities mature in one day, how it compares with a liquid fund, and who uses it for parking money.
items.short: An overnight fund is a debt mutual fund that invests only in securities maturing in one business day, mainly tri-party repos and reverse repos.
body: Overnight funds sit at the lowest end of the risk spectrum among SEBI's debt fund categories. Every day the fund lends its money for one night, mostly through TREPS (tri-party repo on government securities) on the Clearing Corporation of India platform, and gets it back the next morning. Because the loans are collateralised by government securities and last one day, both credit risk and interest rate risk are minimal.

Returns closely follow the overnight money market rate, which in turn tracks the RBI's policy corridor. When the RBI raises or cuts rates, overnight fund yields change almost immediately. Over a year, returns are usually a little lower than a liquid fund's because the fund gives up the small extra yield on 30–90 day paper.

Overnight funds have no exit load and, like liquid funds, publish NAV for every calendar day. Corporates and businesses use them to park cash for a few days, for example between receiving payments and paying salaries. Individuals sometimes use them for the portion of an emergency fund they may need very quickly.
Do not mistake low risk for no risk. Operational and counterparty issues are extremely unlikely but not impossible, and returns can fall below inflation.
items.example: A small trading firm receives ₹50 lakh on Thursday and must pay suppliers the next Tuesday. It invests the money in an overnight fund at an annualised yield of about 6%. Over five calendar days the fund earns roughly ₹50,00,000 × 6% × 5 ÷ 365 ≈ ₹4,110 before tax. The money would otherwise have sat idle in a current account earning nothing.
faqs: What is the difference between an overnight fund and a liquid fund?

An overnight fund holds only one-day securities, so it has almost no interest rate or credit risk. A liquid fund can hold instruments up to 91 days, including commercial paper, giving slightly higher returns with slightly more risk. Liquid funds also carry a small graded exit load for six days; overnight funds usually have none.
Are overnight funds suitable for long-term investing?

Generally no. Their returns track short-term interest rates and are likely to be lower than inflation plus taxes over long periods. They are designed for parking money for days or weeks, not for goals several years away.

items.title: Debt Mutual Fund Meaning: Types, Risks and Taxation
items.description: Debt fund meaning: how debt mutual funds earn returns, the 16 SEBI categories, interest rate and credit risk, and how gains are taxed as of 2026.
items.short: A debt mutual fund invests in fixed-income securities such as government securities, treasury bills, corporate bonds and money market instruments, earning interest and price changes.
body: Debt funds pool money to buy bonds and money market paper. Returns come from two sources: interest accruing on the holdings and changes in their market prices. When interest rates fall, existing bond prices rise and NAVs go up; when rates rise, NAVs fall. The longer the portfolio's duration, the bigger this effect.

SEBI's 2017 categorisation created 16 debt categories, defined by duration (overnight, liquid, ultra short, low, money market, short, medium, medium to long, long), by credit quality (corporate bond, credit risk, banking and PSU) or by issuer (gilt, gilt with 10-year constant duration), plus dynamic bond and floater funds. Each scheme must also disclose a potential risk class matrix showing its maximum interest rate and credit risk.

The two main risks are interest rate risk and credit risk, the chance that an issuer delays or defaults. Liquidity risk matters too: some bonds are hard to sell in a hurry. The 2020 closure of six debt schemes by one AMC showed what can happen when all three combine.

Many investors treat debt funds as fixed deposits. They are not guaranteed, NAV can fall, and as of 2026 gains on debt funds bought after 1 April 2023 are taxed at slab rate regardless of holding period. Check current tax rules before comparing with FDs.
items.example: A medium duration fund has a portfolio Macaulay duration of about 4 years and modified duration of about 3.7. If market yields on similar bonds rise by 0.50 percentage point, the NAV would fall by roughly 3.7 × 0.5% ≈ 1.85%. An investor with ₹4 lakh in the fund would see the value dip by about ₹7,400, partly offset over time by higher accrual at the new yields.
faqs: Can a debt mutual fund give negative returns?

Yes. If interest rates rise sharply, longer duration funds can show losses over short periods. If an issuer defaults, the fund marks the bond down and NAV falls immediately. Over longer holding periods, accrual usually outweighs price changes in good-quality portfolios, but nothing is assured.
How are debt funds taxed in India?

As of 2026, for units of specified debt-oriented funds bought on or after 1 April 2023, all gains are taxed at the investor's slab rate with no indexation, whatever the holding period. Older units may follow earlier rules. Tax law changes frequently, so confirm with the income tax department's current guidance.

items.title: Hybrid Mutual Fund Meaning: Types and Equity Limits
items.description: Hybrid fund types explained: aggressive, conservative, balanced, equity savings and multi-asset funds, with SEBI's equity limits and tax angle.
items.short: A hybrid mutual fund invests in a mix of asset classes, typically equity and debt and sometimes gold, in proportions defined by its SEBI category.
body: Hybrid funds give investors a ready-made asset allocation inside one scheme. SEBI recognises several types. Aggressive hybrid funds keep 65–80% in equity and the rest in debt. Conservative hybrid funds invest 10–25% in equity and mostly in debt. Balanced hybrid funds keep 40–60% each in equity and debt with no arbitrage allowed. Equity savings funds combine equity, arbitrage positions and debt. Multi asset allocation funds invest in at least three asset classes with at least 10% in each. Dynamic asset allocation or balanced advantage funds can move between equity and debt freely. Arbitrage funds are also classified as hybrid.

The fund manager rebalances internally, which is convenient for investors who might otherwise forget to rebalance. Rebalancing inside the fund also does not trigger capital gains tax for the investor.

Taxation depends on the equity share. Schemes that keep at least 65% in domestic equity, including hedged arbitrage positions, are treated as equity-oriented. Others fall under different rules that have changed in recent years, so check current provisions.
A common mistake is assuming 'hybrid' means low risk. An aggressive hybrid fund with 75% equity can fall almost as much as an equity fund in a crash. Look at the category and actual allocation.
items.example: Suresh invests ₹10 lakh in an aggressive hybrid fund holding 70% equity and 30% debt. If equities fall 20% and debt gains 2% in a bad year, the fund would fall roughly (0.70 × −20%) + (0.30 × 2%) = −13.4%, or about ₹1.34 lakh. A conservative hybrid fund with 20% equity would fall roughly (0.20 × −20%) + (0.80 × 2%) = −2.4% in the same year.
faqs: Which hybrid fund is suitable for a first-time investor?

It depends on the investor's time horizon and comfort with losses, which is why suitability assessment matters. Conservative hybrids suit those wanting mild equity exposure; aggressive hybrids suit longer horizons. A SEBI-registered investment adviser or distributor should consider your risk profile before recommending a category.
Are hybrid funds taxed like equity funds?

Only if the scheme keeps at least 65% of assets in domestic equity, which includes hedged equity in some categories. Aggressive hybrid, equity savings and many balanced advantage funds typically qualify; conservative hybrid funds do not. Check the scheme's stated tax treatment and current law.

items.title: Balanced Advantage Fund Meaning: Dynamic Asset Allocation
items.description: How balanced advantage funds shift between equity and debt using valuation models, what net equity means, and the risks of this hybrid category.
items.short: A balanced advantage fund, also called a dynamic asset allocation fund, is a hybrid scheme that changes its mix of equity and debt based on a pre-defined model or market valuations.
body: SEBI's category allows a dynamic asset allocation fund to hold anywhere from 0% to 100% in equity or debt. In practice most Indian balanced advantage funds use a valuation-based model, often price-to-earnings or price-to-book ratios of the Nifty, sometimes combined with trend indicators. When markets look expensive, net equity is reduced; when they look cheap, it is raised.

Many BAFs keep gross equity above 65% so the fund qualifies for equity taxation, but use derivatives (arbitrage or hedges) to bring net, unhedged equity much lower. The factsheet shows both gross and net equity; net equity is what drives the fund's market sensitivity.
The appeal is behavioural: the fund buys low and sells high systematically, without the investor needing to time markets. It suits investors who want equity participation with smaller drawdowns.

The risk is model risk. Valuation signals can stay 'expensive' for years, keeping the fund underweight equity during a strong rally, so it may lag pure equity funds for long periods. Different AMCs' BAFs behave very differently, so comparing them only by name is a mistake.
items.example: A BAF holds ₹1,000 crore. When Nifty valuations are high, its model sets net equity at 35%. The fund holds ₹700 crore in stocks (70% gross equity) but sells index futures worth ₹350 crore as a hedge, so unhedged exposure is ₹350 crore. If the market falls 10%, the portfolio loses roughly 3.5% from equity, not 7%. When valuations later drop, the model lifts net equity, say to 70%.
faqs: What is net equity in a balanced advantage fund?

Net equity is the portion of the portfolio fully exposed to stock market movements after subtracting hedged positions. A fund may show 70% gross equity but only 35% net equity if half is offset by derivatives. Net equity tells you how the fund will move if the market rises or falls.
Can balanced advantage funds lose money?

Yes. They aim to reduce volatility, not eliminate it. With net equity above zero they will fall in market declines, and a debt portion can lose value if rates rise. They may also underperform equity funds during long rallies if the model keeps equity low.

items.title: Arbitrage Fund Meaning: How Cash-Futures Arbitrage Works
items.description: Arbitrage fund explained with an example: buying shares in cash and selling futures, why returns track short-term rates, and how tax treatment works.
items.short: An arbitrage fund is a hybrid mutual fund that earns returns by simultaneously buying a stock in the cash market and selling its futures at a higher price, capturing the price difference.
body: In the stock market, a share's futures contract usually trades above its spot price; the gap reflects the cost of carry until expiry. An arbitrage fund buys the share and sells the futures in equal quantity. At expiry, both prices converge, and the fund locks in the gap regardless of whether the share rises or falls. It then rolls the position into the next month.

SEBI requires arbitrage funds to invest at least 65% in equity and equity-related instruments, almost all of it hedged. The rest sits in debt and money market securities. Because the equity is hedged, market risk is very small, and returns broadly track short-term interest rates.

Tax treatment is the main attraction. Since gross equity exceeds 65%, the fund is treated as equity-oriented, so gains held over a year are taxed as equity LTCG rather than at slab rate. This makes it popular with investors in high tax brackets for parking money for a few months or more.

Returns are not fixed. When markets are quiet and few traders want leveraged long positions, the futures premium shrinks and arbitrage returns fall, sometimes below liquid funds. There is also a typical exit load for very short holding, often around 30 days.
items.example: A stock, call it ABC, trades at ₹2,000 in the cash market and its one-month future at ₹2,011. The fund buys 500 shares for ₹10,00,000 and sells the future for ₹10,05,500. At expiry, if the share closes at ₹1,900, the fund loses ₹50,000 on the shares but gains ₹55,500 on the futures, netting ₹5,500. If it closes at ₹2,100, it gains ₹50,000 and loses ₹44,500, again ₹5,500. That is 0.55% for the month, about 6.6% annualised, before costs.
faqs: Are arbitrage funds risk-free?

No. Market risk is largely hedged, but returns vary with the futures premium and can drop when arbitrage opportunities narrow. There is also execution risk, small credit risk on the debt portion, and exit loads for short holding. They are low-volatility funds, not guaranteed-return products.
Why are arbitrage funds taxed as equity?

Tax law treats a scheme as equity-oriented if at least 65% of its assets are in domestic listed equity. Arbitrage funds meet this test through their hedged stock holdings, so they get equity capital gains treatment even though their risk resembles a short-term debt fund.

items.title: Large Cap Fund Meaning: Top 100 Companies and Risk
items.description: What a large cap fund is under SEBI's rules, how AMFI ranks the top 100 companies by market cap, its 80% equity requirement and how it behaves.
items.short: A large cap fund is an equity mutual fund that must invest at least 80% of its assets in large cap companies, defined as the 100 largest listed companies by full market capitalisation.
body: SEBI's 2017 categorisation fixed precise definitions of large, mid and small cap. AMFI publishes a list every six months ranking all listed companies by average full market capitalisation. Ranks 1 to 100 are large cap, 101 to 250 mid cap, and 251 onward small cap. Large cap funds can keep up to 20% in other stocks or debt.

Large companies are typically market leaders with diversified businesses and better access to capital, such as major banks, IT firms and consumer goods companies. Their share prices tend to be less volatile than smaller companies, and the stocks are highly liquid, so funds can buy and sell large amounts without moving prices much.

The universe is narrow and widely researched, so it is harder for active managers to beat the benchmark after costs. That is why many investors compare a large cap fund with a Nifty 50 or Nifty 100 index fund before choosing.
'Large cap' does not mean safe. In 2008 and early 2020, large cap funds fell 30–50% from peak to trough. They are less volatile than mid and small cap funds, but still carry full equity market risk.
items.example: A large cap fund with AUM of ₹20,000 crore must hold at least ₹16,000 crore in stocks ranked 1–100 on AMFI's list. Suppose a stock it owns slips from rank 98 to rank 104 in the next half-yearly list. The fund does not need to sell immediately; SEBI allows a rebalancing window after the list is published so that the portfolio returns within limits.
faqs: How is a large cap company defined in India?

SEBI defines large cap as the 1st to 100th company by full market capitalisation. AMFI publishes the ranked list twice a year, in January and July, based on average market cap over the preceding six months. Funds use this list to classify holdings.
Is a large cap fund suitable for beginners?

Large cap funds are often seen as a starting point for equity investing because they are less volatile than mid and small cap funds. But they can still fall sharply in market downturns. Suitability depends on time horizon and risk profile, so a holding period of five years or more is commonly suggested.

items.title: Small Cap Fund Meaning: Risks, Rules and Liquidity
items.description: Small cap mutual fund meaning: companies ranked 251 and below, the 65% allocation rule, higher volatility, liquidity stress tests and suitability.
items.short: A small cap fund is an equity mutual fund that invests at least 65% of its assets in small cap companies, those ranked 251st and below by market capitalisation.
body: Small cap companies are younger or niche businesses with room to grow several times over, which is why small cap funds have delivered some of the highest long-term returns in good periods. The same features make them risky: earnings are less stable, management depth is thinner and research coverage is limited.

Liquidity is the hidden risk. Many small cap stocks trade in small volumes. If many investors redeem at once, the fund may have to sell holdings at depressed prices. Since 2024, AMFI and SEBI have required AMCs to disclose stress test results showing how many days it would take to liquidate a set portion of the portfolio. Some AMCs have also restricted lump sum inflows into small cap funds when valuations ran high.

Drawdowns can be severe. Small cap indices in India have fallen more than 50% from peak in past bear markets and taken years to recover. A long holding period, often suggested as seven years or more, and a SIP approach help investors ride these swings.
Investors often chase small cap funds after a year of very high returns. Recent performance is a poor guide; small caps move in long cycles.
items.example: Two investors each put ₹2 lakh into a small cap fund at a market peak. A year later the fund is down 35%, worth ₹1.3 lakh. Investor A panics and redeems, locking in a ₹70,000 loss. Investor B continues a ₹10,000 monthly SIP through the fall, buying units cheaply. If the fund recovers to its old peak NAV in three years, B's earlier lump sum is back to ₹2 lakh and every SIP unit bought below that level shows a gain.
faqs: What is the minimum holding period for a small cap fund?

There is no legal minimum apart from any exit load period. But because small caps are volatile and move in long cycles, many advisers suggest small cap funds only for goals seven or more years away, and only for a part of the equity allocation.
What is a stress test in small cap funds?

It is a disclosure that estimates how many days a fund would need to sell a stated share of its portfolio, such as 25% or 50%, under normal market volumes. More days indicates lower liquidity. AMCs publish these results periodically on their websites and AMFI's.

items.title: Flexi Cap Fund Meaning: How It Differs from Multi Cap
items.description: Flexi cap fund explained: at least 65% in equity with full freedom across large, mid and small caps, and how it differs from a multi cap fund.
items.short: A flexi cap fund is an equity mutual fund that must invest at least 65% in equities but can allocate freely across large, mid and small cap companies.
body: SEBI introduced the flexi cap category in November 2020, after it tightened the rules for multi cap funds. Many funds that had been running as multi cap with mostly large cap holdings shifted to flexi cap to retain their freedom. The fund manager decides how much to put in each market cap segment and can change the mix as opportunities change.

This flexibility is the category's strength and its risk. A skilled manager can tilt toward mid and small caps when they are cheap and back to large caps when they are expensive. A poor call, or style drift, can hurt returns. Investors should check the factsheet periodically to see actual allocation.
Flexi cap funds are often used as a core holding because a single fund gives diversified exposure across the market. They are benchmarked against broad indices such as Nifty 500 TRI or BSE 500 TRI.

Do not confuse flexi cap with multi cap. Multi cap funds must hold at least 25% each in large, mid and small caps; flexi cap funds have no such minimums. Two flexi cap funds can therefore have very different risk profiles.
items.example: On ₹10,000 crore of AUM, Flexi Cap Fund A holds 75% large cap, 18% mid cap, 4% small cap and 3% cash. Flexi Cap Fund B, same category, holds 45% large cap, 30% mid cap and 23% small cap. In a year when small caps fall 25% and large caps fall 8%, Fund B's mix would typically fall noticeably more than Fund A's, even though both carry the same category label.
faqs: What is the difference between flexi cap and multi cap funds?

A multi cap fund must invest at least 25% each in large, mid and small cap stocks, so it always has meaningful small cap exposure. A flexi cap fund only needs 65% in equity overall and can choose any mix across market caps. Flexi cap gives the manager more discretion.
Is a flexi cap fund good as a single core fund?

Many investors use one as a core equity holding because it covers the whole market and lets the manager adjust allocation. Whether it suits you depends on your goals, risk profile and other holdings. Check the fund's actual cap allocation and consistency rather than relying on the category name.

items.title: Multi Cap Fund Meaning: 25% Each in Large, Mid, Small
items.description: Multi cap fund under SEBI rules: minimum 75% equity with at least 25% each in large, mid and small caps, and what this means for risk.
items.short: A multi cap fund is an equity mutual fund that must invest at least 75% in equities, with a minimum of 25% each in large cap, mid cap and small cap stocks.
body: Before 2021, a multi cap fund only needed 65% in equity with no cap-wise limits, and most such funds were dominated by large caps. SEBI changed the rules from January 2021 to ensure the category truly spans the market. Funds that did not want mandatory small cap exposure moved to the new flexi cap category.

The fixed allocation makes multi cap funds more predictable. At least a quarter of the portfolio is always in small caps and a quarter in mid caps, so the fund typically carries higher volatility than a large cap or most flexi cap funds, along with higher potential return over long periods.
The fund manager still has discretion over the remaining 25% of equity and the up to 25% outside equity. Benchmarks such as the Nifty 500 Multicap 50:25:25 index reflect the structure.

Investors sometimes think a multi cap fund is automatically the most diversified choice. It is diversified across market caps, but its mandatory small cap allocation means it can fall sharply in small cap sell-offs, and it may face liquidity constraints when AUM is large.
items.example: A multi cap fund with ₹4,000 crore AUM must hold at least ₹1,000 crore each in large, mid and small caps, and at least ₹3,000 crore in equity overall. Suppose it holds 40% large, 27% mid, 28% small and 5% cash. If small caps fall sharply and that slice drops to 23% of the portfolio, the manager must rebalance back to at least 25% within SEBI's permitted window.
faqs: Why did SEBI change multi cap fund rules?

Many multi cap funds held mostly large cap stocks, so investors did not get the spread across market caps the name suggested. SEBI made the 25% minimums mandatory from 2021 so that the category matches its label, and created flexi cap for funds wanting full freedom.
Is a multi cap fund riskier than a flexi cap fund?

Often, though not always. A multi cap fund must keep at least 25% in small caps and 25% in mid caps, while a flexi cap fund may hold mostly large caps. So a typical multi cap fund carries more small and mid cap risk. Compare actual portfolios to be sure.

items.title: Sectoral and Thematic Funds: Meaning, Risks, Examples
items.description: Sectoral vs thematic mutual funds: 80% in one sector or theme, concentration risk, timing difficulty, and where such funds fit in a portfolio.
items.short: A sectoral or thematic fund is an equity mutual fund that invests at least 80% of its assets in one sector, such as banking or pharma, or one theme, such as infrastructure or consumption.
body: A sectoral fund focuses on a single industry: banking and financial services, IT, pharma, FMCG. A thematic fund takes a broader idea that cuts across sectors, such as manufacturing, ESG, PSU companies, consumption or international technology. Both fall in the same SEBI category and must keep at least 80% in their chosen area.

Concentration is the defining feature. Returns depend heavily on whether that sector does well. IT funds shone in 2020–21 and lagged afterwards; infrastructure funds struggled for much of the 2010s. The fund manager cannot move out of the sector even if its outlook worsens.

Because of this, many advisers treat sectoral and thematic funds as satellite holdings, a small share of the portfolio added to a diversified core, and only for investors who understand and can monitor the sector cycle. Riskometers for these funds are usually 'Very High'.

A common trap is buying a thematic NFO because the theme is in the news. By the time a theme is widely talked about, much of the good news may already be in prices. Another is unknowingly doubling up: a banking fund on top of a large cap fund that is already heavy in banks.
items.example: Rahul has ₹10 lakh in equity funds: ₹8 lakh in a flexi cap fund and ₹2 lakh in a pharma fund. His flexi cap fund already holds about 6% in pharma stocks, so his total pharma exposure is roughly (8 × 6%) + 2 = ₹2.48 lakh, about 25% of his equity. If pharma stocks fall 30%, he loses about ₹74,000 from that sector alone.
faqs: What is the difference between a sectoral and a thematic fund?

A sectoral fund invests in one industry, such as banking. A thematic fund invests in companies linked by an idea that can span sectors, such as consumption, which includes FMCG, autos and retail. SEBI places both in one category with the same 80% minimum.
Should sectoral funds be a large part of a portfolio?

Most advisers keep them small because of concentration risk and the difficulty of timing sector cycles. They can complement a diversified portfolio for informed investors. Suitability depends on the individual's risk profile, so treat this as general information, not advice.

items.title: NFO Meaning in Mutual Funds: How a New Fund Offer Works
items.description: What a new fund offer is, how long an NFO stays open, why ₹10 NFO units are not cheaper, and what to check before investing in a new scheme.
items.short: A new fund offer (NFO) is the first subscription window of a newly launched mutual fund scheme, when units are usually issued at a face value of ₹10.
body: When an AMC launches a scheme, it files the scheme information document with SEBI and then opens an NFO. Under SEBI rules an NFO generally cannot stay open for more than 15 days. Units are allotted after the offer closes, and an open-ended scheme then reopens for continuous purchase and redemption at NAV within a few business days, as SEBI prescribes.

During the NFO, the price is usually ₹10 per unit because the scheme has no portfolio yet. This leads to the biggest myth: that an NFO at ₹10 is cheaper than an existing fund at ₹200. It is not. Your ₹1 lakh buys 10,000 units in the NFO or 500 units of the older fund, and both rise or fall with their portfolios. The face value tells you nothing about value.

Before investing in an NFO, ask whether it offers something your existing funds do not: a new index, a new category or a genuinely different strategy.
