Clients can complain to the adviser, then through SEBI's SCORES platform and the online dispute resolution mechanism. SEBI can take regulatory action, including penalties or cancellation of registration. Documentation of advice is important for both sides.

items.title: Core and Satellite Portfolio Strategy: Meaning, Example
items.description: How the core-satellite approach combines a low-cost diversified core with smaller satellite bets in themes or active funds, with an Indian example.
items.short: A core and satellite portfolio puts most of the money in a stable, diversified, low-cost core and a smaller portion in satellite holdings that seek extra return.
body: The core, often 70–80% of the portfolio, aims for market returns with low cost and low maintenance. Typical core holdings are broad index funds, large cap or flexi cap funds, and high-quality debt funds. The core is held for the long term and rebalanced periodically.

Satellites, the remaining 20–30%, are where the investor or adviser takes specific views: a mid or small cap fund, a sectoral or thematic fund, international equity, a specialised strategy or individual stocks. Satellites can be changed more often and are expected to be more volatile.

The structure limits damage from wrong calls. If a thematic fund in the satellite falls 40%, the whole portfolio drops much less. It also controls cost, since the expensive active or niche products sit only in the satellite. Many advisers find it helps clients who want 'some excitement' without risking the main plan.

Mistakes include letting satellites grow until they dominate, choosing satellites that duplicate the core (a large cap fund as satellite to a Nifty 50 core), and treating the core as boring and neglecting its rebalancing.
items.example: Kunal builds a ₹15 lakh equity portfolio: core of ₹11.25 lakh (75%) split between a Nifty 50 index fund and a Nifty Next 50 index fund, and satellites of ₹3.75 lakh (25%) in a small cap fund and a banking sector fund. If both satellites fall 30%, the loss is about ₹1.13 lakh, or 7.5% of the portfolio, while the core continues tracking the broad market.
faqs: What should be in the core of a portfolio?

Usually broad, diversified, low-cost holdings that suit the investor's long-term allocation: index funds or diversified equity funds and high-quality debt. The core should be something the investor is comfortable holding through market cycles with minimal changes.
How large should the satellite portion be?

Commonly 10–30% of the portfolio, depending on risk profile and experience. The more volatile or concentrated the satellite holdings, the smaller this share should be. The key is that a satellite failure should not derail the investor's goals.

items.title: Modern Portfolio Theory (MPT): Meaning and Example
items.description: Modern portfolio theory explained simply: how correlation lets diversification cut risk, the efficient frontier, and the theory's real-world limits.
items.short: Modern Portfolio Theory (MPT), developed by Harry Markowitz, shows how combining assets with less-than-perfect correlation can reduce portfolio risk for a given expected return.
body: Markowitz's 1952 insight was that an asset should not be judged in isolation. What matters is how it changes the risk and return of the whole portfolio. Risk is measured by standard deviation, and the key ingredient is correlation: how closely two assets move together.

If two assets are perfectly correlated, combining them does not reduce risk; portfolio risk is just the weighted average. If correlation is lower, the ups of one partly offset the downs of the other, and portfolio risk falls below the weighted average. This is the mathematical basis of diversification.

By testing all possible combinations, one can plot the efficient frontier: the set of portfolios giving the highest expected return for each level of risk. A rational investor should hold a portfolio on this frontier, choosing the point that matches their risk tolerance. Adding a risk-free asset leads to the capital market line and later to the capital asset pricing model.

MPT relies on estimates of returns, volatility and correlations from the past, which can change, especially in crises when correlations rise. It also assumes investors care only about mean and variance. Still, its core lesson, that correlation drives the benefit of diversification, underpins modern asset allocation.
items.example: An investor splits money 50:50 between equity (expected return 12%, standard deviation 18%) and debt (7%, 6%). Expected portfolio return is 9.5% whatever the correlation. If correlation were +1, portfolio standard deviation would be 12%, the simple average. With correlation of 0.2 it falls to about 10.0%, and with −0.2 to about 8.9%. Same return, less risk, purely from combining assets that do not move together.
faqs: What is the efficient frontier?

It is the curve showing portfolios that offer the highest expected return for each level of risk, or the lowest risk for each level of return. Portfolios below the curve are inefficient because another combination gives more return for the same risk.
Is modern portfolio theory still relevant?

Yes, as a framework. Its central idea, that combining assets with low correlation reduces risk, guides asset allocation everywhere. But practitioners know its inputs are uncertain and correlations shift in crises, so they use it with judgement rather than as a precise formula.

items.title: Standard Deviation in Mutual Funds: Volatility Explained
items.description: What standard deviation tells you about a mutual fund's volatility, how it is calculated from returns, how to read it in a factsheet, with an example.
items.short: Standard deviation measures how widely a fund's returns are spread around their average; a higher figure means more volatile, less predictable returns.
body: To calculate it, take a series of returns (say monthly returns over three years), find the average, measure how far each return is from the average, square these differences, average them and take the square root. Factsheets usually report annualised standard deviation, which for monthly data is the monthly figure multiplied by the square root of 12.

If returns are roughly normally distributed, about two-thirds of outcomes fall within one standard deviation of the average and about 95% within two. A fund with average return 12% and standard deviation 15% could reasonably see years anywhere from −18% to +42%.
Standard deviation is the risk input in the Sharpe ratio and in modern portfolio theory. Advisers use it to compare funds within a category and to explain to clients what range of outcomes to expect.

Its limitations: it treats upside and downside surprises the same, it understates the chance of extreme events, and it is backward-looking. A debt fund can show very low standard deviation for years and then fall sharply after a credit default. Use it alongside measures like maximum drawdown.
items.example: Over five years, Fund A returned 18%, −6%, 24%, 9% and −2%; average 8.6%, sample standard deviation about 12.8%. Fund B returned 10%, 8%, 12%, 9% and 11%; average 10%, standard deviation about 1.6%. Fund A's investors lived through a 6% loss year and a 24% gain year, while Fund B's had a much smoother ride and a higher average too.
faqs: What is a good standard deviation for a mutual fund?

There is no absolute good figure; it depends on the asset class. Liquid funds show very low numbers, equity funds much higher. Compare a fund with its category average and benchmark over the same period, and consider it with returns using ratios like Sharpe.
Is standard deviation the same as risk?

It is one measure of risk, specifically volatility. It does not capture the risk of permanent loss, credit defaults, liquidity problems or the risk of not meeting a goal. Investors should look at several measures and at what the fund actually holds.

items.title: Risk-Adjusted Return Meaning: Sharpe, Treynor, Sortino
items.description: What risk-adjusted return means, why two funds with equal returns can differ, and how Sharpe, Treynor, Sortino and Jensen's alpha measure it.
items.short: Risk-adjusted return measures how much return an investment produced relative to the risk it took, allowing fair comparison between investments with different volatility.
body: Raw returns can mislead. A fund that earned 15% while swinging wildly may have exposed investors to far more pain than one that earned 13% steadily. Risk-adjusted measures put both on a common footing by dividing excess return by some measure of risk.

The main measures are: Sharpe ratio, excess return over the risk-free rate divided by standard deviation (total risk); Treynor ratio, excess return divided by beta (market risk only); Sortino ratio, excess return divided by downside deviation, which penalises only negative volatility; and Jensen's alpha, the return above what beta would predict. Information ratio, used for active managers, divides active return by tracking error.

Advisers use these measures to shortlist funds within a category, to check whether a manager's outperformance came from skill or just extra risk, and to explain trade-offs to clients. NISM investment adviser and research analyst exams test the formulas.

All of them depend on the period chosen and on past data. A fund can look excellent on a three-year Sharpe that excludes a crash year. Use several measures over rolling periods, and remember that risk-adjusted return does not tell you whether a fund is suitable for a particular client.
items.example: Over three years, with a risk-free rate of 7%: Fund X returned 15% with standard deviation 18% and beta 1.2; Fund Y returned 13% with standard deviation 12% and beta 0.9. Sharpe: X = 8 ÷ 18 = 0.44, Y = 6 ÷ 12 = 0.50. Treynor: X = 8 ÷ 1.2 = 6.67, Y = 6 ÷ 0.9 = 6.67. Y is better on total risk; on market risk alone the two are equal.
faqs: Which risk-adjusted measure is best?

Each answers a different question. Sharpe suits evaluating a whole portfolio's total risk. Treynor suits well-diversified portfolios. Sortino focuses on downside. Information ratio evaluates active managers versus benchmarks. Using two or three together gives a more complete picture.
Why do two funds with the same return have different Sharpe ratios?
Because they took different amounts of risk. The fund with lower volatility gets a higher Sharpe ratio for the same excess return, indicating it delivered that return more efficiently.

items.title: CAGR Meaning, Formula and Calculation with Example
items.description: CAGR explained: the formula for compound annual growth rate, how to calculate it for a lump sum investment, and why it differs from average return.
items.short: Compound Annual Growth Rate (CAGR) is the constant yearly rate at which an investment would have to grow to go from its starting value to its ending value over a period.
body: The formula is CAGR = (ending value ÷ beginning value)^(1 ÷ number of years) − 1. It smooths out year-to-year fluctuations into one annual figure, which makes it easy to compare investments held for different lengths of time. Mutual fund returns for periods over one year are typically shown as CAGR.

CAGR is different from the simple average of annual returns. If an investment rises 50% one year and falls 50% the next, the average return is 0%, but you have actually lost 25% (₹100 becomes ₹150, then ₹75). The CAGR is about −13.4% a year, which reflects reality.

CAGR suits a single lump sum with no further investments or withdrawals. For SIPs or irregular cash flows, CAGR is misleading because different amounts were invested for different periods; XIRR is the right tool there.

A CAGR figure also hides the path. Two funds with 12% CAGR over five years may have had very different volatility along the way. And CAGR for a short period, such as 1.5 years, can look extreme; be careful annualising returns for periods under a year.
items.example: Shalini invested ₹1,00,000 in a fund in April 2019. In April 2025 it was worth ₹2,00,000. CAGR = (2,00,000 ÷ 1,00,000)^(1/6) − 1 = 2^(0.1667) − 1 ≈ 12.25% a year. The absolute return is 100%, but spreading it over six years gives the more comparable annual figure.
faqs: What is the difference between CAGR and absolute return?

Absolute return is the total percentage gain over the whole period, regardless of length. CAGR converts it into an annual compounded rate. A 50% absolute return over 2 years is about 22.5% CAGR; over 5 years it is about 8.4% CAGR.
Can CAGR be used for SIP returns?

Not accurately. In a SIP, each instalment is invested for a different length of time, so a single start and end value does not represent the investment. XIRR accounts for the timing of each cash flow and is the standard measure for SIP returns.

items.title: XIRR Meaning in Mutual Funds: How to Calculate SIP Returns
items.description: What XIRR is, why it is used for SIP and irregular investments, how to calculate it in Excel, and why it differs from absolute return.
items.short: XIRR, or extended internal rate of return, is the annualised return on a series of investments and withdrawals made on different dates, used especially for SIPs.
body: XIRR finds the single annual rate that, applied to every cash flow from its own date, makes the total present value equal to zero. Outflows (investments) are entered as negative numbers and inflows (current value or redemptions) as positive. Spreadsheets have a built-in XIRR function that takes the amounts and dates.

It solves a problem CAGR cannot. In a 12-month SIP, the first instalment was invested for a year but the last for only a month. Dividing total gain by total investment ignores this and understates the real annual return. XIRR weighs each instalment by the time it was invested.

Mutual fund statements, consolidated account statements and most investment apps report SIP returns as XIRR. Advisers use it to measure the actual return of a client's portfolio including additional purchases and withdrawals.

XIRR over very short periods can produce extreme annualised numbers, so treat a one-month XIRR with caution. It also reflects the investor's own timing, so two people in the same fund can have very different XIRRs.
items.example: Amit invested ₹10,000 on the 5th of every month from January to December 2025, a total of ₹1,20,000. On 5 January 2026 his holding is worth ₹1,30,000. Absolute return is ₹10,000 ÷ ₹1,20,000 = 8.3%. But since the average rupee was invested for only about six and a half months, the XIRR works out to roughly 15.7% a year. In a spreadsheet: list the twelve dates with −10,000 and the final date with +1,30,000, then use =XIRR(amounts, dates).
faqs: Why is XIRR higher than absolute return for SIPs?

Because absolute return treats all money as invested for the whole period. In a SIP, later instalments were invested for much less time. XIRR annualises the return based on how long each rupee was actually invested, so for short periods it is usually higher than the absolute percentage.
What is the difference between XIRR and IRR?

IRR assumes cash flows occur at regular intervals, such as every year. XIRR handles cash flows on any dates, which suits real-world investing where SIP dates, extra purchases and withdrawals are irregular. For evenly spaced flows, both give similar answers.

items.title: Time Value of Money: Meaning, Formula and Examples
items.description: Time value of money explained with present value and future value formulas, Indian examples, and why ₹1 lakh today is worth more than ₹1 lakh later.
items.short: Time value of money is the principle that a rupee today is worth more than a rupee in the future, because today's rupee can be invested to earn a return.
body: If you can earn 8% a year, ₹1,00,000 today becomes ₹1,08,000 in a year. So receiving ₹1,00,000 next year is worth less than receiving it today. Inflation reinforces the idea: the same amount buys less in future.

Two formulas capture the principle. Future value: FV = PV × (1 + r)^n, where r is the rate per period and n the number of periods. Present value: PV = FV ÷ (1 + r)^n, which discounts a future amount back to today. Annuity formulas extend this to regular payments such as SIPs, EMIs and pensions.

Time value of money is the foundation of financial planning. It is used to calculate how much to save for a goal, to compare a lump sum with a series of payments, to value bonds, and to decide whether to take a pension or commutation. NISM adviser exams test FV, PV and annuity calculations.

A common error is ignoring the time value when comparing offers. A policy that 'returns ₹10 lakh after 20 years for ₹5 lakh paid' sounds like doubling money, but in time-value terms that is only about 3.5% a year.
items.example: A company offers Ramesh either ₹1,00,000 in five years or ₹70,000 today. If he can earn 8% a year, the present value of ₹1,00,000 in five years is ₹1,00,000 ÷ 1.08^5 ≈ ₹68,058. Since ₹70,000 today is worth more than that, taking the money now is better at that rate. If his expected return were 6%, the present value would be about ₹74,726, and waiting would be better.
faqs: What is the difference between present value and future value?

Future value tells you what an amount invested today will grow to at a given rate. Present value tells you what a future amount is worth today, by discounting it at a given rate. They are the same formula rearranged.
Which discount rate should be used for present value?

Use the return you could reasonably earn on an alternative investment of similar risk, often called the opportunity cost. For a safe future payment, a government bond or bank deposit rate is common. For risky cash flows, a higher rate is used.

items.title: Behavioural Finance Meaning: Common Investor Biases
items.description: What behavioural finance studies, key biases such as loss aversion, herd behaviour, anchoring and overconfidence, and how advisers help investors avoid them.
items.short: Behavioural finance studies how psychological biases and emotions lead investors to make decisions that depart from rational, purely financial reasoning.
body: Traditional finance assumes investors are rational and markets efficient. Behavioural finance, built on work by Daniel Kahneman, Amos Tversky and Richard Thaler, shows that real people use mental shortcuts that often lead them astray, especially under uncertainty and stress.

Key biases include: loss aversion, feeling losses about twice as strongly as equal gains, which leads to selling winners too early and holding losers too long; herd behaviour, buying what everyone else is buying, as in NFO and small cap frenzies; anchoring, fixating on a reference price such as the purchase price; overconfidence, overestimating one's ability to pick stocks or time markets; recency bias, assuming recent returns will continue; and mental accounting, treating money differently by its source, such as a bonus.

These biases explain why investor returns are often lower than fund returns: people invest after rallies and redeem after falls. Advisers counter them with written plans, automatic SIPs, pre-agreed rebalancing rules and education before markets fall, not during.
Biases are not only for beginners. Professionals suffer them too. Awareness helps but is not enough; systems and rules work better than willpower.
items.example: In early 2020 Vivek's ₹5 lakh equity portfolio fell 35% to ₹3.25 lakh. Fearing further losses, he redeemed everything in April. Markets recovered strongly over the next year, and a similar portfolio broadly tracking the Nifty that stayed invested would have climbed back above ₹5 lakh by early 2021. His friend Sneha had a written plan with a SIP and an annual rebalancing rule; she kept investing and topped up equity during the fall. The same market gave them very different outcomes, purely from behaviour.
faqs: What is herd behaviour in investing?

It is the tendency to follow what others are doing rather than one's own analysis, such as rushing into a hot sector or selling in a panic because everyone is. Herding can push prices far from fair value and often leads to buying high and selling low.
How can investors reduce behavioural biases?

Use rules decided in calm times: a written plan, automatic SIPs, a target asset allocation with rebalancing bands, and limits on checking portfolios daily. Working with a registered adviser can also add accountability during emotional market phases.

items.title: Loss Aversion Bias in Investing: Meaning and Examples
items.description: Loss aversion explained: why investors feel losses more than gains, how it causes the disposition effect and panic selling, and practical fixes.
items.short: Loss aversion is the behavioural tendency to feel the pain of a loss more strongly than the pleasure of an equal gain, often by around twice as much.
body: Kahneman and Tversky's prospect theory found that most people would reject a coin toss offering a ₹1,000 loss or a ₹1,500 gain, even though the expected value is positive. Losses loom larger than gains. This asymmetry shapes many investment mistakes.

One result is the disposition effect: investors sell winning holdings quickly to 'lock in' gains but hold losing ones for years, hoping to get back to the purchase price. Another is panic selling in market falls, when the pain of watching losses becomes unbearable. Loss aversion also makes people keep too much in fixed deposits and too little in equity for long-term goals, accepting a near-certain erosion by inflation to avoid visible fluctuations.

Advisers handle it by framing: showing how often equity has been negative over 1, 5 and 10 years rather than only daily moves; separating short-term money from long-term money so falls in the latter are less frightening; and agreeing in advance what to do in a crash.
Loss aversion is not the same as sensible risk aversion. Avoiding risk you cannot afford is prudent; avoiding all visible losses at the cost of long-term goals is the bias.
items.example: Neeraj bought shares of Company P at ₹800 and Company Q at ₹500. P rises to ₹1,000 and Q falls to ₹350. Needing ₹50,000, he sells P because booking a 'profit' feels good and holding Q avoids 'accepting' a loss. Yet Q's prospects have weakened. Selling Q would also have produced a capital loss that could be set off against gains. His decision followed feelings, not analysis.
faqs: How does loss aversion affect mutual fund investors?

It leads many to stop SIPs or redeem during market falls, exactly when units are cheapest, and to wait until markets recover before investing again. Over time this lowers their actual returns compared with the fund's own returns.
Is loss aversion always harmful?

Some caution is healthy and protects against reckless bets. It becomes harmful when it causes decisions that hurt long-term goals, such as holding failing investments to avoid booking a loss or keeping retirement money entirely in low-return assets.

items.title: Power of Compounding Meaning with Examples in Rupees
items.description: How compounding works when returns earn returns, why starting early matters more than investing more later, with ₹ examples for lump sums and SIPs.
items.short: Compounding is the process by which an investment's returns are reinvested and themselves earn returns, so that wealth grows faster over time than with simple interest.
body: With simple interest, ₹1 lakh at 10% earns ₹10,000 every year. With compounding, the second year's 10% is earned on ₹1.1 lakh, the third year's on ₹1.21 lakh, and so on. The growth curve bends upward: most of the final value comes in the later years.

Three variables drive compounding: the amount invested, the rate of return and, above all, time. Because time sits in the exponent of the formula FV = P × (1 + r)^n, adding years has a far bigger effect than adding a little to the return or the amount. This is why advisers urge young earners to start a modest SIP early rather than a large one at 40.

Compounding works in reverse too. Costs, inflation and high-interest debt compound against you. A credit card balance at 36–42% a year doubles in about two years if unpaid, and a 1% higher expense ratio compounds into a large shortfall over decades.

Compounding requires staying invested and reinvesting returns. Withdrawing gains, choosing IDCW payouts and spending them, or stopping SIPs during market falls all break the chain. Returns in equity are not steady, so the smooth curves in brochures are illustrations, not promises.
items.example: ₹1,00,000 invested at 10% a year compounds to about ₹2.59 lakh in 10 years, ₹6.73 lakh in 20 years and ₹17.45 lakh in 30 years. The last 10 years add more than the first 20 combined. Similarly, ₹10,000 a month for 20 years at an assumed 12% (monthly compounding) grows to about ₹1 crore on an investment of ₹24 lakh.
faqs: Why is starting early so important for compounding?

Because time is the exponent in the compounding formula. Someone who invests ₹5,000 a month from 25 to 35 and then stops may end up with a similar or larger amount at 60 than someone who invests ₹5,000 a month from 35 to 60, at the same return, despite investing far less money.
What is the difference between simple and compound interest?

Simple interest is calculated only on the original principal. Compound interest is calculated on the principal plus previously earned interest. Over short periods the difference is small; over long periods compound interest produces dramatically larger amounts.

items.title: Rule of 72: How Fast Will Your Money Double?
items.description: The rule of 72 explained: divide 72 by the annual return to estimate years to double, with examples for FDs, equity and inflation, and its accuracy.
items.short: The rule of 72 is a quick mental shortcut: divide 72 by the annual rate of return to estimate how many years it takes for money to double.
body: At 8% a year, money doubles in about 72 ÷ 8 = 9 years. At 12%, in about 6 years. The rule works because of the mathematics of compounding; the precise doubling time is ln(2) ÷ ln(1 + r), and 72 gives a close approximation for typical interest rates between about 6% and 10%.

It can be used in reverse: to double money in 5 years, you need roughly 72 ÷ 5 = 14.4% a year. It also applies to anything that compounds, including inflation and debt. At 6% inflation, the purchasing power of money halves in about 12 years.

The rule is popular in financial education and competitive exams because it gives an instant sense of scale without a calculator. Variants exist: the rule of 114 estimates tripling time and the rule of 144 estimates quadrupling.

Remember that the rule assumes a constant compounded return. Equity returns vary year to year, so for equity it gives only a rough idea. At very high rates, such as 30%, the rule becomes less accurate; 72 ÷ 30 = 2.4 years versus the true 2.64 years.
items.example: Neha has ₹5 lakh in a fixed deposit at 7%. By the rule of 72 it doubles in about 72 ÷ 7 ≈ 10.3 years (the exact figure is about 10.2 years). If inflation runs at 6%, prices also double in about 12 years. So in real terms her FD barely grows. An equity fund averaging 12% would double in about 6 years, though with much more year-to-year variation.
faqs: How accurate is the rule of 72?

Very close for returns between about 6% and 10%, within a few months. At low rates (2–3%) or high rates (above 20%) the error grows. Some people use 69 or 70 for continuous compounding. For exact figures, use a calculator with the compounding formula.
Can the rule of 72 be used for inflation?

Yes. Divide 72 by the inflation rate to estimate how long it takes for prices to double, or equivalently for your money's purchasing power to halve. At 6% inflation, ₹1 lakh will buy only what about ₹50,000 buys today in roughly 12 years.

items.title: Real Rate of Return: Inflation-Adjusted Return Explained
items.description: Learn the difference between nominal and real return, the exact formula, why post-tax real return matters, and an FD example with inflation.
items.short: The real rate of return is the return on an investment after adjusting for inflation, showing the actual increase in purchasing power.
body: A nominal return is what the investment statement shows, say 7% on a fixed deposit. If prices rise 5% over the same year, your money buys only about 1.9% more than before. That is the real return. The quick approximation is nominal return minus inflation; the exact formula is (1 + nominal) ÷ (1 + inflation) − 1.

For planning, the post-tax real return is what matters. Interest on FDs is taxed at slab rate, so a 7% FD for someone in the 30% slab (plus cess) yields about 4.8% after tax, which may be below inflation. In that case the investor is losing purchasing power even though the balance grows.

Financial planners use real returns to project goals in today's rupees and to choose asset classes. Over long periods, equity has historically delivered a positive real return in India, while many fixed-income products have hovered close to inflation after tax.
A common error is comparing returns from different periods without adjusting for the inflation of those periods. A 10% return when inflation was 9% is worse than 7% when inflation was 3%.
items.example: Gopal has ₹10 lakh in a 7% FD and is in the 30% tax slab (31.2% with cess). Pre-tax real return at 5% inflation = 1.07 ÷ 1.05 − 1 ≈ 1.9%. After tax, his interest is 7% × (1 − 0.312) ≈ 4.82%. Real post-tax return = 1.0482 ÷ 1.05 − 1 ≈ −0.17%. His deposit grows in rupees but slightly shrinks in purchasing power.
faqs: Can real return be negative?

Yes, whenever inflation is higher than the nominal return, or higher than the post-tax return. Savings accounts and some fixed deposits often show negative real returns after tax, which slowly erodes purchasing power even though the balance grows.
Which inflation figure should I use for real return?

For general use, the consumer price index (CPI) is the standard measure in India. For specific goals, use the relevant inflation, such as education or medical costs, which have often risen faster than CPI. Personal inflation also varies by lifestyle.

items.title: Emergency Fund Meaning: How Much to Keep and Where
items.description: What an emergency fund is, how many months of expenses to keep, where to park it (savings, sweep FD, liquid fund), and common mistakes to avoid.
items.short: An emergency fund is money set aside in safe, easily accessible form to cover unexpected expenses or loss of income without breaking long-term investments or borrowing.
body: Job loss, medical emergencies not fully covered by insurance, urgent home repairs or a family crisis can all demand cash quickly. Without a buffer, people swipe credit cards, take personal loans at high rates or redeem equity funds at the worst time. An emergency fund is the first building block of any financial plan, before investing for goals.

A common guideline is three to six months of essential expenses, including EMIs and insurance premiums. Self-employed people, those with irregular income, single-income families and people in volatile industries often keep 9–12 months. The figure is based on expenses, not income.

Safety and liquidity matter more than return. Typical places are a savings account, a sweep-in fixed deposit, and liquid or overnight mutual funds. Many people split it: one month's expenses in the savings account for instant access, the rest in a sweep FD or liquid fund that can be accessed within a day.

Mistakes include investing the emergency fund in equity, counting a credit card limit as an emergency fund, and failing to rebuild it after use. Health insurance is separate; an emergency fund is not a substitute for adequate cover.
items.example: Farida's monthly essentials are ₹40,000: rent ₹15,000, groceries and utilities ₹12,000, EMI ₹8,000, insurance and transport ₹5,000. Six months' cover means ₹2.4 lakh. She keeps ₹40,000 in her savings account, ₹1 lakh in a sweep-in FD and ₹1 lakh in a liquid fund. When her father needs a ₹60,000 medical procedure, she uses the savings balance and the FD without touching her equity SIPs.
faqs: Should an emergency fund be invested in mutual funds?

Part of it can be, in liquid or overnight funds, which are low-risk and usually redeemable within a business day. Equity funds are unsuitable because they can be down sharply when you need the money. Keep some in a bank account for immediate access.
How do I build an emergency fund quickly?

Set a target, automate a monthly transfer into a separate account, and direct windfalls like bonuses or tax refunds to it. Cutting discretionary spending for a few months helps. Pause new long-term investments only if needed, and continue term and health insurance.

items.title: Net Worth Meaning: How to Calculate Your Net Worth
items.description: Personal net worth explained: total assets minus liabilities, what to include and exclude, an Indian worked example, and why tracking it matters.
items.short: Net worth is the total value of everything a person owns minus everything they owe, giving a snapshot of their overall financial position.
body: Assets include bank balances, fixed deposits, mutual funds, shares, EPF and PPF balances, NPS, gold, real estate at realistic market value, and the surrender value (not sum assured) of insurance policies. Liabilities include outstanding home loan, car loan, personal loans, education loans and credit card balances.

Planners often separate financial assets from lifestyle assets. A self-occupied house and a car add to net worth on paper but do not generate income or fund goals unless sold. Calculating 'investable net worth' excluding them gives a clearer view of what can support retirement.

Tracking net worth once or twice a year shows whether you are actually getting wealthier. A rising salary with a flat net worth means spending or debt is absorbing the gains. A falling net worth during a market dip is less worrying than one falling because of new borrowings.

Common mistakes: counting a term insurance sum assured as an asset; using the purchase price of property instead of a realistic sale value; ignoring small loans and card dues; and comparing net worth with friends rather than with your own goals.
items.example: Rajiv, 36, lists assets: savings and FDs ₹4 lakh, mutual funds ₹11 lakh, EPF ₹9 lakh, PPF ₹3 lakh, gold ₹2 lakh and a flat worth ₹70 lakh, totalling ₹99 lakh. Liabilities: home loan ₹48 lakh, car loan ₹3 lakh and card dues ₹50,000, totalling ₹51.5 lakh. Net worth = ₹99 lakh − ₹51.5 lakh = ₹47.5 lakh. Excluding the flat and its loan, his investable net worth is ₹29 lakh − ₹3.5 lakh = ₹25.5 lakh.
faqs: Should my house be included in net worth?

Include it for total net worth, at a realistic sale value, along with the home loan as a liability. For retirement and goal planning, many advisers also compute investable net worth excluding the home you live in, since it will not generate cash unless sold or rented.
How often should I calculate my net worth?
Once or twice a year is enough for most people. Tracking it monthly can lead to over-reacting to market movements. Compare against your own past figures and goals rather than with others.

items.title: 50-30-20 Rule of Budgeting: Meaning and Indian Example
items.description: The 50-30-20 budget rule explained: needs, wants and savings split of take-home pay, how to adapt it for Indian cities, EMIs and early-career earners.
items.short: The 50-30-20 rule is a simple budgeting guideline that splits take-home income into 50% for needs, 30% for wants and 20% for savings and debt repayment.
body: Needs are expenses you must pay to live and work: rent or home loan EMI, groceries, utilities, basic transport, insurance premiums, school fees and minimum loan payments. Wants are discretionary: eating out, entertainment, travel, gadgets, shopping beyond basics, subscriptions. Savings include SIPs, PPF, emergency fund contributions and extra loan prepayments.

The rule became popular through US personal finance writing, and it works as a starting framework rather than a law. In high-rent Indian cities, needs may take 60% of a young professional's income. Those with family responsibilities may need a different split. Many planners suggest raising savings to 25–30% when possible, especially once salaries rise.

Its value is in simplicity. It gives a quick check on whether lifestyle spending is crowding out savings, without tracking every rupee. Automating the savings portion on salary day, the 'pay yourself first' habit, makes the rule work.

Mistakes include classifying wants as needs (a premium phone plan or a car upgrade), applying percentages to gross salary instead of take-home pay, and not adjusting as income grows. Note that EPF deducted from salary is already a form of saving.
items.example: Ankit, 26, takes home ₹80,000 a month in Pune. Under 50-30-20: needs ₹40,000 (rent ₹18,000, food and utilities ₹12,000, transport ₹4,000, insurance and family support ₹6,000), wants ₹24,000, savings ₹16,000. He sets up SIPs of ₹12,000 and an RD of ₹4,000 for his emergency fund on the 2nd of each month, so the savings happen before spending begins.
faqs: Is 20% savings enough?

It is a reasonable minimum for many people, but those starting late, with ambitious goals or high incomes may need to save more, often 25–40%. Goal-based calculations show the actual savings needed. The 50-30-20 rule is a starting point, not a target for everyone.
Where do EMIs fit in the 50-30-20 rule?

Minimum EMI payments on essential loans like a home loan are generally treated as needs. Extra prepayments count toward the savings portion. EMIs for lifestyle purchases, such as a gadget on a no-cost EMI, are better treated as wants.

items.title: Retirement Corpus Meaning: How Much Do You Need?
items.description: How to estimate a retirement corpus in India: inflating today's expenses, choosing a multiple or annuity approach, and common planning mistakes.
items.short: A retirement corpus is the total sum of money a person needs to have accumulated by retirement to fund living expenses for the rest of their life.
body: Estimating it starts with today's annual expenses that will continue after retirement, excluding costs like children's education or home loan EMIs that will end, and adding new ones like higher medical spending. These expenses are inflated to the retirement date. Then the planner estimates how much money is needed at retirement to fund those expenses, rising with inflation, for 25–30 years or more.

A quick rule of thumb is 25 to 33 times first-year retirement expenses, linked to the idea of a sustainable withdrawal rate of 3–4%. A more precise method uses the present value of a growing annuity, with an assumed post-retirement return and inflation. Pensions, EPF, NPS and rental income reduce the corpus required from personal savings.

The biggest risks are underestimating inflation, especially medical inflation, underestimating life expectancy, and assuming high returns after retirement. Sequence-of-returns risk, where markets fall just after retirement, can also damage a corpus.
Many people underestimate the corpus because they think in today's rupees. Planners show figures in both future and today's terms to make them meaningful.
items.example: Suresh, 35, spends ₹50,000 a month (₹6 lakh a year) and plans to retire at 60. At 6% inflation, his annual expenses at retirement would be about ₹6 lakh × 1.06^25 ≈ ₹25.75 lakh. Using a 25-times rule, his target corpus is about ₹6.4 crore. In today's rupees that is about ₹1.5 crore, which helps him grasp the scale. His EPF and NPS balances will count toward this.
faqs: How much money is enough to retire in India?

It depends on your expenses, lifestyle, inflation, life expectancy, pension and other income. A rough approach is 25–33 times your first-year retirement expenses. A registered adviser or retirement adviser can build a detailed projection with realistic assumptions.
Should my retirement corpus be fully in debt after retirement?

Usually not. Retirement may last 25–30 years, during which inflation erodes fixed-income returns. Many planners keep a portion in equity for growth, with several years of expenses in safer assets to avoid selling equity during downturns.

items.title: Safe Withdrawal Rate and the 4% Rule Explained
items.description: What a safe withdrawal rate is, where the 4% rule came from, why Indian retirees may need a lower rate, and how to apply it with an example.
items.short: A safe withdrawal rate is the percentage of a retirement corpus that can be withdrawn in the first year, then increased with inflation, without the money running out over retirement.
body: The best-known version is the 4% rule, based on research by William Bengen in the 1990s using US market history. It found that withdrawing 4% of the starting portfolio, adjusted for inflation each year, would have lasted at least 30 years in almost all historical periods for a balanced stock-bond portfolio.

The rule cannot be copied blindly to India. Indian inflation has historically been higher than US inflation, and retirements may last longer than 30 years for someone retiring at 55. Many Indian planners therefore use 3–3.5% as a more conservative starting point.

The safe rate depends on asset allocation, fees, taxes, flexibility in spending and the sequence of returns early in retirement. Retirees who can cut spending in bad years can start at a higher rate. Those with pensions covering basic needs can afford more risk.

The rule is a planning tool, not a guarantee. It is also often misunderstood: 4% is the first-year amount, which then rises with inflation, not 4% of whatever the corpus is each year. Annual reviews help adjust withdrawals to actual results.
items.example: Lata retires at 60 with ₹2 crore. Using a 4% rule, she withdraws ₹8 lakh in year one. If inflation is 6%, she withdraws ₹8.48 lakh in year two, ₹8.99 lakh in year three, and so on, regardless of market performance. At a more conservative 3.5%, she would start at ₹7 lakh. She keeps about three years of withdrawals in debt funds and runs an SWP from there.
faqs: Is the 4% rule safe in India?

It is a rough guide derived from US data. Higher inflation and potentially longer retirements in India mean many planners suggest starting lower, around 3–3.5%, and reviewing every year. A retirement adviser can test withdrawal rates against your specific situation.
What if markets fall early in retirement?

This is sequence-of-returns risk. Withdrawals from a falling portfolio deplete it faster. Holding several years of expenses in safer assets, reducing withdrawals temporarily and avoiding selling equity during falls help protect the corpus.

items.title: LTCG Tax Meaning: Long-Term Capital Gains in India
items.description: Long-term capital gains explained: holding periods for equity and other assets, the 12.5% equity LTCG rate and ₹1.25 lakh exemption as of 2026, with example.
items.short: Long-term capital gain (LTCG) is the profit from selling a capital asset, such as shares, mutual fund units or property, after holding it longer than the period specified by tax law.
body: Whether a gain is long or short term depends on the holding period. As of 2026, listed equity shares and equity-oriented mutual funds become long term after 12 months; most other assets, including property and unlisted shares, after 24 months. Debt mutual fund units bought on or after 1 April 2023 are taxed at slab rate regardless of holding period, so the long-term label gives no benefit there.

For listed equity and equity-oriented funds, LTCG above an annual exemption (₹1.25 lakh per financial year as of 2026) is taxed at 12.5% plus cess, without indexation. Gains on equity bought before 1 February 2018 are 'grandfathered': the cost is taken as the higher of actual cost and the market value on 31 January 2018, subject to conditions. For most other long-term assets the rate is 12.5% without indexation, with transitional options for property bought before July 2024.
These rates changed in the July 2024 Budget, and the Income-tax Act, 2025 replaces the 1961 Act from April 2026 with renumbered sections. Always check the income tax department's current guidance.
Common confusion: the exemption applies to total equity LTCG across all holdings in a year, not per fund. Each SIP instalment has its own holding period.
items.example: Meera sells equity fund units in FY 2025-26 bought three years earlier, making a gain of ₹3,00,000. She has no other equity LTCG that year. Taxable LTCG = ₹3,00,000 − ₹1,25,000 = ₹1,75,000. Tax at 12.5% = ₹21,875, plus 4% cess = ₹22,750. Had she spread redemptions over two financial years, she could have used the exemption twice. (Rates as of 2026; check current law.)
faqs: Is LTCG on mutual funds tax-free up to ₹1.25 lakh?

For equity-oriented funds and listed shares, as of 2026, long-term gains up to ₹1.25 lakh in aggregate per financial year are exempt; tax at 12.5% applies above that. The exemption is per person per year across all such assets. Debt fund gains do not get this exemption. Check current law.
How is the holding period counted for SIPs?

Each SIP instalment is a separate purchase with its own date. When you redeem, units are taken on a first-in-first-out basis. Some units may be long term and others short term, so the gain is split accordingly.

items.title: STCG Tax Meaning: Short-Term Capital Gains Explained
items.description: Short-term capital gains explained: when gains are short term, the 20% rate on listed equity as of 2026, slab-rate STCG on others, and set-off rules.
items.short: Short-term capital gain (STCG) is the profit from selling a capital asset held for a period shorter than the threshold set by tax law for long-term treatment.
body: For listed equity shares and equity-oriented mutual funds, units sold within 12 months produce STCG. As of 2026, such gains, where securities transaction tax is paid, are taxed at a flat 20% plus cess, regardless of the investor's slab. This rate rose from 15% in July 2024.

For other assets, such as property held under 24 months, gold funds, or unlisted shares, STCG is added to income and taxed at the investor's slab rate. Debt fund units bought after 1 April 2023 are taxed at slab rate whatever the holding period.

Short-term capital losses can be set off against both short-term and long-term capital gains in the same year, and unabsorbed losses can be carried forward for eight years if the return is filed on time. Long-term losses can be set off only against long-term gains.

Two practical points: the basic exemption limit can absorb STCG for residents with low income, and there is no annual exemption for equity STCG like the one for LTCG. Tax rules change frequently, and the Income-tax Act, 2025 renumbers sections from April 2026, so verify current provisions.
items.example: Arjun buys equity fund units for ₹2,00,000 in June 2025 and sells them in February 2026 for ₹2,80,000, an STCG of ₹80,000. Tax at 20% = ₹16,000, plus 4% cess = ₹16,640. If he had waited until after June 2026, the gain would have been long term and, if within the ₹1.25 lakh exemption with no other equity gains, possibly tax-free. (Rates as of 2026; check current rules.)
faqs: What is the STCG tax rate on mutual funds?

As of 2026, equity-oriented funds sold within 12 months are taxed at 20% plus cess. Debt funds bought after 1 April 2023 are taxed at slab rate regardless of holding period. Hybrid and other funds depend on their equity share. Check current income tax rules for your case.
Can short-term capital losses reduce long-term gains?

Yes. A short-term capital loss can be set off against both short-term and long-term capital gains in the same year. A long-term loss, however, can only be set off against long-term gains. Unused losses can be carried forward for up to eight years if returns are filed on time.

items.title: Indexation Benefit Meaning: CII and Capital Gains
items.description: What indexation means in capital gains tax, how the cost inflation index adjusts purchase cost, where it still applies after 2024, with an example.
items.short: Indexation is the adjustment of an asset's purchase cost for inflation using the government's Cost Inflation Index (CII), which reduces the taxable long-term capital gain.
body: Inflation means part of any long-term gain is not a real gain at all. Indexation addresses this by raising the purchase cost in line with inflation. Indexed cost = original cost × (CII of the year of sale ÷ CII of the year of purchase). The CII is notified by the Central Board of Direct Taxes each year, with 2001-02 as the base year at 100.

Until July 2024, indexation was available for many long-term assets, including debt mutual funds bought before April 2023, gold, and property, usually with a 20% tax rate on the indexed gain. The July 2024 Budget removed indexation for most assets and moved to a flat 12.5% rate without indexation.

A transitional choice remains for land or buildings acquired before 23 July 2024 by resident individuals and HUFs: they can pay the lower of 12.5% without indexation or 20% with indexation. Indexation still matters in exams, in older cases and in this property option. The Income-tax Act, 2025 replaces the 1961 Act from 1 April 2026 and renumbers sections, so the familiar section name may now map to a new reference; check the income tax department's current guidance.
A common confusion: indexation never applied to listed equity shares or equity-oriented mutual funds, which have their own LTCG regime.
items.example: Kiran bought a gold investment for ₹1,00,000 in FY 2015-16 (CII 254) and sold it for ₹1,60,000 in FY 2023-24 (CII 348), under the old rules. Indexed cost = ₹1,00,000 × 348 ÷ 254 ≈ ₹1,37,008. Indexed LTCG = ₹1,60,000 − ₹1,37,008 = ₹22,992. At 20%, tax was about ₹4,598 before cess. Without indexation at the current 12.5% on the full ₹60,000 gain, tax would be ₹7,500, illustrating why the change matters.
faqs: Is indexation still available on debt mutual funds?

For debt fund units bought on or after 1 April 2023, gains are taxed at slab rate without indexation. For older units, the July 2024 changes removed indexation and set a flat 12.5% on long-term gains from that date. Transitional rules can be complex, so check current law.
What is the Cost Inflation Index?

The CII is a number notified by the CBDT each financial year to reflect inflation. With 2001-02 as base 100, it is used to adjust the purchase cost of assets when indexation is allowed. For example, the CII for FY 2023-24 is 348 and for FY 2024-25 is 363.

items.title: Section 80C Deduction: Limit, Eligible Investments, Regime
items.description: Section 80C explained: the ₹1.5 lakh deduction limit as of 2026, eligible investments like PPF, ELSS and EPF, old vs new regime, and a tax example.
items.short: Section 80C is the income tax provision under which individuals and HUFs can reduce taxable income by up to ₹1.5 lakh a year through specified investments and expenses, under the old tax regime.
body: Eligible items include employee contribution to EPF, PPF deposits, ELSS mutual funds, life insurance premiums (within limits relative to sum assured), the principal portion of home loan EMIs, tuition fees for up to two children, five-year tax-saver bank fixed deposits, National Savings Certificates, Sukanya Samriddhi deposits and the Senior Citizens' Savings Scheme. The combined deduction is capped at ₹1.5 lakh a year as of 2026; NPS contributions under related sections share part of this cap.

The deduction is available only under the old tax regime. The new regime, which is the default, does not allow it. Whether 80C matters to you depends on which regime gives lower tax after considering all deductions.

Lock-ins vary widely: three years for ELSS, five years for tax-saver FDs, fifteen years for PPF, and until retirement or job change for EPF. Many salaried people find EPF and home loan principal already use most of the limit, so further 80C purchases add nothing. The Income-tax Act, 2025 replaces the 1961 Act from 1 April 2026 and renumbers sections, so the familiar section name may now map to a new reference; check the income tax department's current guidance.
The most common mistake is buying insurance-linked savings products in March just to save tax, locking money into low-return plans that do not suit the goal.
items.example: Neha, in the old regime with taxable income in the 30% slab, has EPF deductions of ₹72,000 and home loan principal of ₹40,000, totalling ₹1,12,000. She can claim only ₹38,000 more under 80C. Investing ₹38,000 in ELSS or PPF saves about ₹38,000 × 31.2% = ₹11,856 in tax. Investing ₹1 lakh more would not save any additional tax because the cap is reached.
faqs: Can I claim 80C under the new tax regime?

No. As of 2026, the new regime does not allow Section 80C deductions; it offers lower slab rates and a higher standard deduction instead. If your 80C and other deductions are large, the old regime may still be better. Compare both each year.
What is the maximum limit under Section 80C?

The limit is ₹1.5 lakh per financial year for individuals and HUFs as of 2026, combined across all eligible investments and expenses. Additional deductions such as 80CCD(1B) for NPS and 80D for health insurance are separate. Check current law, as limits and section numbers can change.

items.title: Section 80D: Health Insurance Tax Deduction Explained
items.description: Section 80D explained: deduction for health insurance premiums for self, family and parents, higher limits for senior citizens, and a worked example.
items.short: Section 80D allows a deduction from taxable income for health insurance premiums and certain medical expenses paid for oneself, family and parents, under the old tax regime.
body: As of 2026, the deduction for premiums covering self, spouse and dependent children is up to ₹25,000 a year, or ₹50,000 if the policyholder or spouse is a senior citizen. A separate deduction of up to ₹25,000 (₹50,000 for senior citizen parents) is available for premiums paid for parents, whether or not they are dependent. Preventive health check-up expenses up to ₹5,000 are allowed within these limits.

For senior citizens without health insurance, actual medical expenditure up to the senior-citizen limit can be claimed. Premiums must be paid by any mode other than cash, except for preventive check-ups.

The deduction is available only under the old tax regime. Under the new regime there is no 80D deduction, but health insurance remains essential protection, independent of tax. The Income-tax Act, 2025 replaces the 1961 Act from 1 April 2026 and renumbers sections, so the familiar section name may now map to a new reference; check the income tax department's current guidance.
Common confusion: the limits apply per group (self-family and parents), not per policy, and a multi-year premium paid upfront is spread across the years of cover for the deduction.
items.example: Rohit, 38, pays ₹20,000 for a family floater covering himself, his wife and child, and ₹35,000 for his parents, both over 60. Under the old regime he can claim ₹20,000 for his family (limit ₹25,000) and ₹35,000 for his parents (limit ₹50,000), a total of ₹55,000. In the 20% slab, this saves about ₹55,000 × 20.8% = ₹11,440 in tax.
faqs: Can I claim 80D for my parents' health insurance?

Yes, under the old regime. Premiums paid for parents qualify for a separate deduction of up to ₹25,000, or ₹50,000 if either parent is a senior citizen, as of 2026. The parents need not be financially dependent on you. Pay by a non-cash mode.
Is 80D available in the new tax regime?

No. As of 2026 the new regime does not allow 80D deductions. Health insurance remains important for protection regardless of tax savings. Compare both regimes using your actual deductions to see which gives lower tax.

items.title: Section 80CCD(1B): Extra ₹50,000 NPS Tax Deduction
items.description: How Section 80CCD(1B) gives an additional ₹50,000 deduction for NPS contributions under the old regime, how it differs from 80CCD(2), with example.
items.short: Section 80CCD(1B) allows an additional deduction of up to ₹50,000 a year for own contributions to the National Pension System, over and above the Section 80C limit, under the old regime.
body: NPS contributions can be claimed under three provisions. Section 80CCD(1) covers the subscriber's own contribution within the overall ₹1.5 lakh 80C limit. Section 80CCD(1B) gives an exclusive extra deduction of up to ₹50,000 for own NPS Tier I contributions. Section 80CCD(2) covers the employer's contribution to the employee's NPS account, up to a percentage of salary.

80CCD(1B) is available only under the old tax regime as of 2026. The employer contribution deduction under 80CCD(2) is available in both regimes, with a higher percentage limit allowed under the new regime for private sector employees; check current limits.

The deduction makes NPS attractive for taxpayers in higher slabs who have already exhausted 80C. But the money is locked until 60, apart from limited partial withdrawals, and a portion at exit must be used to buy an annuity under PFRDA rules, which is taxable as income. The Income-tax Act, 2025 replaces the 1961 Act from 1 April 2026 and renumbers sections, so the familiar section name may now map to a new reference; check the income tax department's current guidance.
A frequent mistake is contributing to NPS Tier II and expecting the deduction; Tier II is a voluntary account and generally does not qualify.
items.example: Anjali, in the old regime and the 30% slab, has already used ₹1.5 lakh under 80C through EPF and PPF. She contributes ₹50,000 to her NPS Tier I account. Under 80CCD(1B) her taxable income falls by ₹50,000, saving ₹50,000 × 31.2% = ₹15,600 in tax. Her employer also contributes 10% of basic salary to NPS, which she claims separately under 80CCD(2).
faqs: Is 80CCD(1B) part of the ₹1.5 lakh 80C limit?

No. 80CCD(1B) is an additional deduction of up to ₹50,000 over and above the ₹1.5 lakh limit, available only for own contributions to NPS Tier I and only under the old regime as of 2026. Check current law for any changes.
Can I claim NPS deduction in the new tax regime?

Only the employer's contribution under 80CCD(2) is allowed in the new regime, as of 2026. Your own contributions under 80CCD(1) and 80CCD(1B) are not deductible there. Salaried employees can ask employers about NPS through salary restructuring.

items.title: Standard Deduction for Salaried: Meaning and Limits
items.description: Standard deduction explained: the flat deduction for salaried people and pensioners, ₹75,000 in the new regime and ₹50,000 in the old as of 2026.
items.short: Standard deduction is a flat amount that salaried employees and pensioners can subtract from their salary or pension income before tax, without showing any proof of expenses.
body: Standard deduction was reintroduced in 2018 in place of separate transport and medical allowances. It is automatic: employers factor it into TDS, and taxpayers claim it in their return without bills or investments. Family pension recipients have a separate, smaller deduction.

As of 2026, the standard deduction is ₹75,000 under the new tax regime and ₹50,000 under the old regime. The new-regime figure was raised in the July 2024 Budget. Under the new regime, combined with the rebate, salaried individuals with income up to about ₹12.75 lakh pay no income tax for FY 2025-26, subject to conditions.

Standard deduction applies only to income under the head 'salaries' (including pension). Freelancers and business owners do not get it; they deduct actual business expenses instead. The Income-tax Act, 2025 replaces the 1961 Act from 1 April 2026 and renumbers sections, so the familiar section name may now map to a new reference; check the income tax department's current guidance.

A common error is thinking standard deduction is a tax saving of ₹75,000. It reduces taxable income; the actual tax saved depends on your slab. At a 10% marginal rate, ₹75,000 of deduction saves about ₹7,500 plus cess.
items.example: Priya earns a salary of ₹12,75,000 in FY 2025-26 under the new regime with no other income. After the ₹75,000 standard deduction, taxable income is ₹12,00,000. As of 2026 the tax on this, after the rebate available up to ₹12 lakh, is nil. Her colleague earning ₹13,00,000 has taxable income of ₹12,25,000, above the rebate threshold, and pays some tax subject to marginal relief. (Check current rules.)
faqs: Do I need to submit proof for standard deduction?
No. It is a flat deduction given automatically to salaried employees and pensioners. Your employer applies it while calculating TDS, and you claim it in the return without documents.
Is standard deduction available in both tax regimes?

Yes. As of 2026 it is ₹75,000 under the new regime and ₹50,000 under the old regime for salaried individuals and pensioners. Limits are revised in budgets from time to time, so confirm the current figures.

items.title: Old vs New Tax Regime: Differences and How to Choose
items.description: Old vs new income tax regime explained: slab rates, deductions allowed, which suits whom, and a worked comparison for a ₹15 lakh salary as of 2026.
items.short: India's individual taxpayers can choose between the old tax regime, with higher rates but many deductions, and the new regime, with lower rates but few deductions; the new regime is the default.
body: The old regime allows deductions such as 80C (₹1.5 lakh), 80D for health insurance, 80CCD(1B) for NPS, house rent allowance, leave travel allowance and home loan interest on a self-occupied house. Its slab rates rise to 30% above ₹10 lakh of taxable income.

The new regime, made the default from FY 2023-24, has more slabs with lower rates, a higher standard deduction (₹75,000 as of 2026) and a larger rebate, but disallows most deductions. Employer contribution to NPS under 80CCD(2) is still allowed. For FY 2025-26, the slabs run from nil up to ₹4 lakh through 5%, 10%, 15%, 20% and 25% to 30% above ₹24 lakh.

Salaried taxpayers can choose each year. Those with business income can switch back to the old regime only in limited circumstances. The right choice depends on how large your deductions are. As a rough pattern, people with modest deductions now usually pay less under the new regime. The Income-tax Act, 2025 replaces the 1961 Act from 1 April 2026 and renumbers sections, so the familiar section name may now map to a new reference; check the income tax department's current guidance.
Do not choose a regime and then buy investments to justify it. Compute tax both ways using deductions you would claim anyway.
items.example: Vikram earns ₹15 lakh salary in FY 2025-26. Old regime: deductions of ₹50,000 standard, ₹1.5 lakh 80C, ₹25,000 80D and ₹50,000 NPS leave taxable income of ₹12.25 lakh; tax is ₹12,500 + ₹1,00,000 + 30% of ₹2.25 lakh = ₹1,80,000, or ₹1,87,200 with cess. New regime: taxable income ₹14.25 lakh after ₹75,000 standard deduction; tax is ₹20,000 + ₹40,000 + 15% of ₹2.25 lakh = ₹93,750, or ₹97,500 with cess. The new regime saves about ₹89,700 here. (Illustrative; check current slabs.)
faqs: Which tax regime is better for salaried employees?

It depends on your deductions. With large HRA, home loan interest and full use of 80C, 80D and NPS, the old regime can still win at some income levels. With few deductions, the new regime is usually better. Calculate tax both ways each year.
Can I switch between old and new tax regimes every year?

Salaried individuals without business income can choose each year while filing the return. Those with business or professional income have limited switching options. Inform your employer of your choice for TDS, though the final choice is made in the return. Check current rules.

items.title: Tax-Loss Harvesting in India: Meaning and Example
items.description: How tax-loss harvesting works for Indian investors: booking capital losses to offset gains, set-off and carry-forward rules, and points of caution.
items.short: Tax-loss harvesting is selling investments that are below their purchase cost to realise a capital loss, which can then be used to reduce taxable capital gains.
body: Capital losses are only recognised for tax when realised by selling. An investor who has booked gains during the year, and also holds investments showing losses, can sell the loss-making holdings before 31 March so that the realised losses offset the gains.

Indian set-off rules, as of 2026: short-term capital losses can be set off against both short-term and long-term gains; long-term capital losses only against long-term gains. Unabsorbed losses can be carried forward for eight assessment years, but only if the income tax return is filed by the due date.

A related strategy, sometimes called tax-gain harvesting, involves booking long-term equity gains up to the annual exemption limit each year and reinvesting, to reset the cost base higher at no tax cost.

Cautions: selling and immediately buying back the same asset may be questioned by tax authorities under anti-avoidance principles, even though India has no specific wash-sale rule like the US; exit loads and transaction costs reduce the benefit; and the main purpose of an investment decision should not be tax alone. Check current law or consult a tax professional.
items.example: In FY 2025-26, Sameer has booked ₹1,00,000 of short-term gains on equity funds. Another equity fund he bought six months ago shows a ₹40,000 unrealised loss. He sells it in March, realising a ₹40,000 short-term loss, which reduces his net STCG to ₹60,000. At 20% plus cess, his tax falls from ₹20,800 to ₹12,480, a saving of ₹8,320. He reinvests in a different fund with similar exposure to stay invested.
faqs: Can capital losses be set off against salary income?

No. Capital losses can only be set off against capital gains, following the short-term and long-term rules. They cannot reduce salary or business income. Unused losses can be carried forward for eight years if the return is filed on time.
Is tax-loss harvesting legal in India?

Realising genuine losses to offset gains is permitted. However, artificial transactions done only to create losses may attract scrutiny under general anti-avoidance principles. Keep transactions genuine and documented, and consult a tax professional for complex cases.

items.title: PPF Account Meaning: Rules, Lock-in, Interest and Tax
items.description: Public Provident Fund explained: 15-year tenure, ₹500 to ₹1.5 lakh yearly limits, partial withdrawals, loans, extensions and EEE tax status as of 2026.
items.short: The Public Provident Fund (PPF) is a government-backed long-term savings scheme with a 15-year tenure, offering tax-free interest and qualifying for Section 80C under the old regime.
body: A PPF account can be opened at a post office or authorised bank by any resident Indian individual, including on behalf of a minor. The minimum deposit is ₹500 a year and the maximum ₹1.5 lakh per financial year, across your own and minor's accounts. The government sets the interest rate every quarter; it has been 7.1% a year for an extended period, but check the current rate.

Interest is calculated on the lowest balance between the 5th and the last day of each month and credited annually, so depositing before the 5th of a month, ideally before 5 April, maximises interest. The account matures after 15 full financial years and can be extended in blocks of five years, with or without fresh deposits.

Liquidity is limited: loans are allowed from the third to the sixth year and partial withdrawals from the seventh year, within limits. Premature closure is permitted after five years only for specified reasons such as serious illness or higher education, with an interest penalty.

PPF has 'EEE' status: deposits qualify for deduction under the old regime, interest is tax-free and maturity is tax-free. The sovereign backing makes it very safe, but the long lock-in makes it unsuitable for short-term goals.
items.example: Kavya deposits ₹1,50,000 every April for 15 years. At an assumed constant 7.1%, compounded annually, her balance at maturity would be about ₹40.7 lakh, of which ₹22.5 lakh is her contribution and about ₹18.2 lakh is tax-free interest. Under the old regime in the 30% slab, each year's deposit also reduces tax by about ₹46,800. Actual rates vary quarterly, so this is illustrative.
faqs: Can I withdraw from PPF before 15 years?

Partial withdrawals are allowed from the seventh financial year, up to a limit linked to earlier balances. Premature closure is allowed after five years only for specific reasons such as serious illness or higher education, with an interest reduction. Loans are available from the third to the sixth year.
Is PPF interest taxable?

No. PPF enjoys EEE status as of 2026: contributions qualify for deduction under the old regime, interest earned is tax-free and the maturity amount is tax-free. Even under the new regime, interest and maturity remain tax-free, though the deposit is not deductible.

items.title: EPF Meaning: Contribution Rules, Interest and Withdrawal
items.description: Employees' Provident Fund explained: 12% contributions, EPS split, interest declared by EPFO, withdrawal and transfer rules, and tax points.
items.short: The Employees' Provident Fund (EPF) is a mandatory retirement savings scheme for salaried employees, managed by EPFO, with contributions from both employee and employer.
body: Establishments with 20 or more employees must register with EPFO. Employees whose basic salary plus dearness allowance is up to ₹15,000 a month must join; others may join voluntarily. The employee contributes 12% of basic plus DA. The employer also contributes 12%, of which 8.33% (on wages up to ₹15,000) goes to the Employees' Pension Scheme (EPS) and the rest to EPF.

EPFO's central board declares the interest rate each year, approved by the government; it was 8.25% for recent years, but check the current rate. Each member has a Universal Account Number (UAN) that stays with them across jobs, making transfers easier.

Partial withdrawals are allowed for purposes such as housing, medical treatment, education and marriage, subject to service conditions, and EPFO has been simplifying these rules. Full withdrawal is allowed on retirement or after a period of unemployment. Withdrawals before five years of continuous service are generally taxable.

Tax: employee contributions qualify for 80C under the old regime. Interest on employee contributions above ₹2.5 lakh a year (₹5 lakh where there is no employer contribution) is taxable. Many employees overlook EPF as their largest retirement asset.
items.example: Rahul's basic plus DA is ₹30,000 a month. He contributes 12% = ₹3,600. His employer contributes ₹3,600: 8.33% of the ₹15,000 wage ceiling, about ₹1,250, goes to EPS, and the remaining ₹2,350 to EPF. So ₹5,950 goes into his EPF account monthly, about ₹71,400 a year, plus EPS credit. His own ₹43,200 annual contribution counts under 80C in the old regime.
faqs: Is EPF withdrawal taxable?

Withdrawal after five years of continuous service, including service with previous employers if the account was transferred, is generally tax-free. Withdrawal before five years is usually taxable, with TDS if above a threshold and PAN conditions. Rules can change, so check EPFO and income tax guidance.
What is the difference between EPF and PPF?

EPF is linked to employment, with mandatory contributions from employee and employer and an interest rate declared annually by EPFO. PPF is a voluntary scheme anyone can open, with a 15-year tenure and a rate set quarterly by the government. Both are long-term, low-risk retirement tools.

items.title: NPS Meaning: National Pension System Tiers, Tax, Exit
items.description: National Pension System explained: Tier I and Tier II, asset choices, PFRDA regulation, tax benefits, and annuity rules at exit as of 2026.
items.short: The National Pension System (NPS) is a voluntary, defined-contribution retirement savings scheme regulated by PFRDA, investing in equity, corporate bonds and government securities.
body: Any Indian citizen aged roughly 18 to 70 can open an NPS account, and it is mandatory for most central and state government employees who joined after 2004. The Tier I account is the pension account, with restrictions on withdrawal and tax benefits. Tier II is a voluntary savings account with easy withdrawals and generally no tax benefit.

Subscribers choose a pension fund manager and either an active choice, setting their own split between equity (E), corporate debt (C), government securities (G) and a small alternative assets class, or an auto choice that reduces equity with age. Equity is capped at a percentage that falls with age. Costs are among the lowest of any retirement product.

Historically, at exit at 60, at least 40% of the corpus had to buy an annuity and up to 60% could be taken as a tax-free lump sum. PFRDA has revised exit and withdrawal rules for some subscriber categories, and government employees now have other options such as the Unified Pension Scheme, so check current PFRDA rules as of 2026. Annuity income is taxable.
Tax benefits under the old regime include deduction within 80C, the extra ₹50,000 under 80CCD(1B), and employer contribution under 80CCD(2), which is also allowed in the new regime.
items.example: Deepak, 30, contributes ₹5,000 a month to NPS Tier I with an auto-choice moderate life cycle fund. Suppose his corpus at 60 is ₹1 crore. Under the historical rule, he could take up to ₹60 lakh as a tax-free lump sum and use ₹40 lakh to buy an annuity; at an illustrative 6.5% annuity rate, that would pay about ₹2.6 lakh a year, taxable as income. Current exit rules should be checked with PFRDA before planning.
faqs: What is the difference between NPS Tier I and Tier II?

Tier I is the main pension account with withdrawal restrictions until retirement and tax benefits. Tier II is an optional voluntary account linked to Tier I, offering flexible withdrawals but generally no tax deductions, except a special case for government employees. You need Tier I to open Tier II.
Can I withdraw NPS money before 60?

Partial withdrawals from Tier I are allowed after a minimum period for specified purposes such as children's education, marriage, house purchase or critical illness, within limits. Premature exit is also possible with a higher annuity requirement. PFRDA revises these rules, so check the latest before planning.

items.title: Sukanya Samriddhi Yojana (SSY): Rules, Interest, Tax
items.description: Sukanya Samriddhi Yojana explained: eligibility for a girl child under 10, deposit limits, 21-year maturity, withdrawals at 18 and EEE tax status.
items.short: Sukanya Samriddhi Yojana (SSY) is a government-backed small savings scheme for a girl child, offering a fixed interest rate set quarterly and tax-free returns.
body: Launched in 2015 under the Beti Bachao Beti Padhao campaign, SSY lets a parent or legal guardian open an account for a girl child below 10 years of age at a post office or authorised bank. Generally up to two accounts per family are allowed, with exceptions for twins or triplets.

The minimum deposit is ₹250 a year and the maximum ₹1.5 lakh per financial year. Deposits are required for 15 years from opening; the account matures 21 years from opening, and the balance continues to earn interest in the remaining years. The government sets the interest rate quarterly; it has been among the highest of small savings schemes, around 8.2% recently, but check the current rate.

Up to 50% of the balance can be withdrawn after the girl turns 18 or passes class 10, for higher education. The account can be closed on her marriage after 18. Like PPF, SSY has EEE tax status: deposits qualify for 80C under the old regime, and interest and maturity are tax-free.
SSY is safe and tax-efficient, but the money is locked for a long time and returns are fixed-income returns. For a goal 18 years away, many families combine it with equity investments.
items.example: Ramesh opens an SSY account for his 1-year-old daughter and deposits ₹1,50,000 each year for 15 years, a total of ₹22.5 lakh. At an assumed constant 8.2% compounded annually, the balance after 15 years would be about ₹44.8 lakh, and with six more years of interest without deposits, about ₹71.8 lakh at maturity when she is 22. faqs: Who can open a Sukanya Samriddhi account?

A parent or legal guardian can open it for a girl child below 10 years of age who is resident in India. Generally a family can open accounts for up to two daughters, with an exception for twins or triplets. Check current rules at the post office or bank.
When can money be withdrawn from SSY?

Up to 50% of the balance at the end of the previous financial year can be withdrawn after the girl turns 18 or passes class 10, for education. Full closure is allowed at maturity, 21 years from opening, or on her marriage after age 18, as per scheme rules.
